Charge order before superconductivity in the doped kagome Dirac spin liquid

Yasir Iqbal  Email: yiqbal@physics.iitm.ac.in Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India
September 25, 2026
Abstract

Doping a quantum spin liquid is expected to produce a superconductor. We show that for the Dirac spin liquid on the kagome lattice the doped charge orders first. The charge is carried by a chargon doublet whose two gauge components are degenerate on the square and triangular lattices, and the kagome lattice, as the line graph of the honeycomb lattice, splits them. One component disperses and condenses in four valleys. The other has flat lowest bands and stays empty over a window in the bare mass whose width, (6−1)​t(\sqrt{6}-1)t, follows from the band structure alone. Within that window, in the mean-field chargon theory constructed from the projective symmetry group of the spin liquid, the doped state forms charge and loop-current crystals with the electromagnetic U(1) unbroken and no superconductivity. Pairing requires a gapped descendant of the spin liquid as the parent and then takes the form of a pair-density wave, with no uniform d+i​dd+id channel at leading order and none at any order for the crystals at the MM point. The predicted charge order is odd under the twofold rotation and has no cubic invariant, which distinguishes it from the charge order of the kagome metals.

I Introduction

The fate of a quantum spin liquid once charge is restored to it is a question nearly as old as the resonating-valence-bond proposal [3]. The expectation that grew from that proposal was that a Mott insulator whose spins form a liquid of singlets becomes a superconductor once doped [2, 74]. This paper works out what doping does to the U(1) Dirac spin liquid of the kagome lattice, within a mean-field treatment that holds the parent fixed, and finds charge order and loop-current order with the electromagnetic U(1) unbroken, over a window that the band structure fixes in closed form. Superconductivity requires a different parent, one of the gapped descendants of the spin liquid, and it then takes the form of a pair-density wave. The lattice geometry decides whether a superconducting channel is available at all, and the interactions select among the condensates that remain.

The chargon construction poses this question in a form controlled by symmetry. One represents the spin liquid by fermionic spinons with a projective symmetry group (PSG) and carries the charge with bosonic chargons [74] that inherit the spinons’ emergent gauge structure. The band minima of the chargon, the projective action of the lattice symmetries on those valleys, and the resulting Landau theory then dictate which conventional orders emerge upon doping or pressure [14, 9]. Because the PSG differs from one lattice to the next, the answer has to be worked out case by case. On the square lattice it yields dd-wave superconductivity intertwined with charge stripes [18]. On the triangular lattice it yields a variety of density waves and finite-momentum superconductors descending from the Dirac spin liquid [31]. In both cases the two components of the chargon gauge doublet are degenerate, so the quartic couplings determine whether a given condensate is a superconductor or a pure density wave, and both occur in those phase diagrams [18, 31]. On kagome the two components are split, because the kagome lattice is the line graph of the honeycomb lattice. The two lowest bands of one gauge component are pinned flat at −2​t-2t, while the other component disperses with four minima at −(1+6)​t-(1+\sqrt{6})t. Only the dispersive component can condense, and it does so over a window in the bare mass of width (6−1)​t(\sqrt{6}-1)t, a separation of band bottoms and not an interacting gap. Within this window the doped Dirac spin liquid orders into charge crystals and loop-current crystals without superconductivity.

The kagome lattice is well studied from both the insulating and the metallic side. On the insulating side, the ground state of the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet remains unsettled among the [0,π][0,\pi] Dirac spin liquid (DSL, Fig. 1) [41, 105, 45], a gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid [134, 23, 91] and a thirty-six-site valence-bond crystal [89, 114]. We take the DSL as the parent. It is the best variational description of the model [52, 54], and signatures of its Dirac cones have been seen in density-matrix renormalization spectra [43], tensor-network calculations [81], and the entanglement response to flux insertion [142]. The leading gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} candidate is, moreover, itself one of its descendants (Sec. V). The central results do not depend on how that debate is resolved, because the moduli-space theorem of Sec. III.3 (through sextic order) and the entire particle–hole composite catalog of Table 2 are identical for the DSL and for all four of its ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants. Herbertsmithite and its analogs are the material realizations [97, 40, 10]. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} neighbors of the DSL have been classified [86], and its chiral neighbor is an established Kalmeyer–Laughlin phase [66, 36, 5, 47, 128, 7]. The doped problem, however, has stood open since Ko, Lee, and Wen proposed an exotic anyon superconductor from the doped kagome liquid [75]. Strong-coupling numerics find insulating crystals of spinless holons at light doping, with no superconductivity there [62, 102, 133]. The one realized electron-doping series, Li intercalation [71], finds an insulator at every composition studied, and Ga substitution leaves the kagome plane undoped because its extra charge is anion-compensated [104]. A systematic symmetry analysis of what doping the kagome DSL can produce has been missing. On the metallic side, the kagome metals AAV3Sb5 and their relatives display 2×22\times 2 charge order, disputed time-reversal breaking, and pair-density-wave superconductivity [24]. Their theoretical description has been built on weak-coupling sublattice interference [73, 129, 130] and on Landau and mean-field theories of the 2×22\times 2 charge and loop-current orders [100, 22, 17, 84, 28, 121, 123, 29], and a link between the itinerant and strong-coupling pictures has been asked for explicitly [24].

The two sides have so far been treated as separate problems. On the insulating side, the idea that competing phases descend from a single low-energy structure, the algebraic spin liquid as the “mother of many competing orders” [46], has been made precise for the kagome lattice. There the U(1) Dirac spin liquid is the parent of its neighbors. The magnetic and valence-bond orders around it are components of a single set of low-energy operators, the fermion bilinears together with the monopoles, whose symmetry quantum numbers follow from the spinon band topology [45, 118, 116]. The near-degeneracy that makes kagome numerics so delicate is then a consequence of that structure and not an accident of the model. On the doped side, the algebraic charge liquid [68] added charge to an algebraic spin liquid through fermionic holons coupled to its gauge field. No counterpart of the classification exists, however, once charge is allowed to fluctuate. The operators that carry charge are absent from the insulating theory by construction, so the superconducting, pair-density-wave, charge-ordered and current-carrying phases that descend from the parent cannot be read off from the monopole spectrum. Yet these are the phases at issue in the doped spin liquid and in the kagome metals. The charge sector has its own multiplet, the projective valley representation of the chargon, and a classification of its own that is fixed by the projective symmetry group alone.

Here we construct that counterpart, the PSG-constrained chargon theory of the kagome DSL, of its four ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants (with translation-invariant spinon pairing), and of its chiral descendant beyond the sector crossing of Sec. VI, at and away from half filling. One chargon gauge component reproduces the holon band of Ref. [75], with four nondegenerate minima at −(1+6)​t-(1+\sqrt{6})t [Fig. 2(a,b)]. The other carries the doubly degenerate flat multiplet of that spectrum as its lowest states, pinned at −2​t-2t, and the splitting Δflat=(6−1)​t\Delta_{\rm flat}=(\sqrt{6}-1)t is the window quoted above. Because only one component condenses, the physical electromagnetic U(1) stays unbroken, and the condensed state is a chargon Higgs phase with no superfluid response. Whether it is metallic, semimetallic or insulating is determined by the spinon spectrum in the condensate-renormalized link field. At mean field all three commensurate condensates are metals. The emergent Gauss law moves the spinons off half filling by the doped density, so the electron-like quasiparticles form Fermi pockets of total Luttinger volume xx around the two Dirac nodes. An insulating gap at the commensurate lock-ins must therefore come from physics beyond mean field (Sec. VII). With no superfluid response, the descendants proper, produced by condensing the chargon, are distinct from the vestigial orders, which are composites of the multiplet that order where superconductivity is absent. The distinction persists to finite temperature, where the leading scale is the condensate stiffness and not a superconducting one.

For the condensing component, the projective symmetry action leaves one quadratic and three quartic invariants, all in closed form, and these reduce the whole quartic competition to a single angle (Fig. 3). The projected on-site repulsion sits on the boundary between the MM-star and K/2K/2-star condensates. This direction, which we call the Hubbard ray, is protected to all orders in the quartic and gauge couplings by an O⁡(4)×U⁡(1)O(4)\times U(1) symmetry of the projected on-site quartic, a symmetry larger than the PSG requires. The MM-star phase hosts a moduli space, the pair sphere of competing charge crystals, which stays degenerate through sextic order and is lifted at octic order, where the octic term derived for on-site repulsion selects the uni-MM stripe.

Pairing requires the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} channels and is then a pair-density wave on the phase-I and II- arcs of Fig. 3, which contain the projected on-site and nearest-neighbor directions. The pairing map of the four ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants admits only one-dimensional uniform channels, one per descendant, namely extended ss (A1A_{1}), the two ff waves (B1B_{1}, B2B_{2}), and A2A_{2}. A uniform d+i​dd+id state is excluded at leading order, because the uniform pair channel of every descendant is one-dimensional and has no E2E_{2} content. It is excluded at every order for the MM-star condensates, whose crystal momenta forbid any uniform pair composite. Beyond a sector crossing, the chiral descendant becomes a two-valley theory with a flat ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} manifold at quartic order. Only intersite loop terms resolve this manifold, and every on-site moment through cubic order is constant on it. Because the chiral state has no spinon pairing, it orders at quartic order as a nonsuperconducting charge and current crystal. The two-valley theory is conditional, since we do not determine whether the doped state lies beyond the crossing. Placing it there requires identifying the chargon links with the spinon links, and the symmetry-allowed intra-hexagon link that this identification brings in closes the sector margin (Sec. VI.2).

The composite orders realize symmetry channels that are new to the kagome problem. In the MM-point irrep labels used for the kagome metals, they include C2C_{2}-odd F3F_{3} charge order with no cubic invariant, F2′F_{2}^{\prime} loop currents, a KK-star loop-current crystal, and K/2K/2-star charge crystals at half the KK wavevector. The DSL’s own operators below scaling dimension two carry only Γ\Gamma- and MM-point momenta, and every MM-triplet among them is C2C_{2}-even. In the insulating theory the C2C_{2}-odd F3F_{3} channel occurs only among the conserved currents, and the KK and K/2K/2 stars do not occur. No chargon channel coincides with a mass or monopole channel, since the spin-singlet MM-triplets of the masses and monopoles are all 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even. The common channels lie in the DSL’s conserved MM-point currents, which contain both F3F_{3} and F2′F_{2}^{\prime} [45, 116, 118], and the mechanisms that produce them differ between the two sectors. The classification needs no enhanced flavor symmetry of the charge sector. The O⁡(4)×U⁡(1)O(4)\times U(1) of the Hubbard ray belongs to one coupling direction and plays no part in it.

The charge and loop-current orders of the weak-coupling theory of the kagome metals and of the present theory of the doped insulator decompose into the same FF irreps of the MM star, so the strong-coupling and weak-coupling descriptions of kagome charge order can be compared directly. They differ in the irrep of the charge order, F1F_{1} for the metals against F3F_{3} here, and in the presence or absence of the Landau cubic, while the F2′F_{2}^{\prime} loop-current channel is common to both. The comparison is one of symmetry classification and does not interpolate between the two limits.

Section VIII turns these results into testable consequences for doped herbertsmithite and for the kagome metals. The charge order is C2C_{2}-odd and transforms as the F3F_{3} irrep of the MM point, so it admits no Landau cubic and no symmetry-mandated first-order transition, whereas the F1F_{1} order of the kagome metals has the opposite parity, a difference accessible to scanned probes and to resonant x-ray scattering at the Cu L3L_{3} edge. The superconductor supported by the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants is a pair-density wave with no uniform component at the quartic level on the branches selected by on-site and nearest-neighbor repulsion, and its vestigial phase has a flux period of h/4​eh/4e or h/6​eh/6e depending on which crystal forms. The loop currents produce local fields of 33 to 2020 G at x=1/36x=1/36 and 1818 to 118118 G at x=1/6x=1/6 at the sites within 33 Å of the kagome plane, reduced by factors of 1.41.4 and 7.07.0 once the local Gauss law is imposed (Appendix B), which still leaves them one to two orders of magnitude above the fields that zero-field μ\muSR reports at the charge-order transitions of the kagome metals, and polar Kerr and anomalous Hall responses are forbidden by symmetry for the single-arm stripe and allowed for the multi-arm crystals. Charge order and loop-current order set in together, at a single transition TCOT_{\rm CO} that our estimates place below a separate chargon condensation scale TρT_{\rho}, provided the Γ\Gamma-point flux orders with the condensate.

The paper proceeds as follows. Section II sets up the parton construction and shows that the chargon band structure splits into two spectrally inequivalent sectors. Section III constructs the projective valley representation, the Landau–Higgs functional, the moduli-space theorem, and the all-orders protection of the Hubbard ray. Section IV maps the condensed phases, including the loop-current stripe manifold of phase I and the K/2K/2 crystals of phase II, and catalogs the composite order parameters. Section V treats the four ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants and their pairing channels, Sec. VI treats the chiral descendant and its two-valley theory, and Sec. VII follows the doped case from Gross–Pitaevskii to strong coupling. Section VIII compares the theory with experiment, and Sec. IX concludes. The appendices collect gauge conventions and verification methodology, proof details, the two-loop check of the ray protection, the four projective symmetry groups, the chiral-ansatz verification, and complete composite tables. Where we call a result exact, we mean a spectral identity of the free chargon problem or a statement of representation theory and invariant algebra, all checked numerically to the tolerances of Appendix A. Where a result depends on the projection onto the condensation valleys or on the classical (mean-field or Gross–Pitaevskii) truncation, we say so.

II Chargon theory of the kagome Dirac spin liquid

II.1 Parton construction and conventions

We represent the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} degrees of freedom by fermionic spinons f𝒊​σf_{{\bm{i}}\sigma}, collected into the Nambu doublet ψ𝒊=(f𝒊↑,f𝒊↓†)⊤\psi_{\bm{i}}=(f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow},f^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow})^{\!\top}, with the quadratic mean-field Hamiltonian H=−∑i​jψ†𝒊ui​jψ𝒋H=-\sum_{ij}\psi^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}}u_{ij}\psi_{\bm{j}}, where the link fields ui​j=uj​i†u_{ij}=u_{ji}^{\dagger} are 2×22\times 2 matrices in the SU(2) gauge space [127]. A U(1) spin liquid is an ansatz whose invariant gauge group is U(1); for the states considered here ui​ju_{ij} commutes with τ3\tau^{3}. A spin-independent spinon hopping −∑i​j​σti​jf†𝒊​σf𝒋​σ-\sum_{ij\sigma}t_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\sigma}f_{{\bm{j}}\sigma} corresponds to ui​j=diag⁡(ti​j,−ti​j∗)=(Re​ti​j)​τ3+i⁡(Im​ti​j)​τ0u_{ij}=\mathrm{diag}(t_{ij},-t_{ij}^{*})=(\mathrm{Re}\,t_{ij})\,\tau^{3}+i\,(\mathrm{Im}\,t_{ij})\,\tau^{0}, with τ0\tau^{0} the unit matrix. It is proportional to τ3\tau^{3} when ti​jt_{ij} is real, as in the time-reversal-symmetric DSL [Eq. (5)], and acquires a τ0\tau^{0} component in the chiral ansatz of Sec. VI. In either case the residual gauge transformations are rotations about τ3\tau^{3}.

Charge fluctuations, relevant both for the doped system and for the charge response of the insulator, are introduced through the SU(2) rotor (chargon) decomposition of the electron [14, 18, 31, 9], which builds on the SU(2) slave-boson formulation of the tt–JJ model [126, 79, 80],

(c𝒊↑c𝒊↓†)=ℬ𝒊†​ψ𝒊,𝒮B⊃∑i​jB𝒊†​ui​j​B𝒋,\begin{pmatrix}c_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}\\ c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{B}^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}}\,\psi_{\bm{i}}\,,\qquad\mathcal{S}_{B}\supset\sum_{ij}B^{\dagger}_{\bm{i}}\,u_{ij}\,B_{\bm{j}}\,, (1)

where ℬ𝒊\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}} is an SU(2) matrix built from the spinless, charge-ee chargon doublet B𝒊=(B𝒊,+,B𝒊,−)⊤B_{\bm{i}}=(B_{{\bm{i}},+},B_{{\bm{i}},-})^{\!\top},

ℬ𝒊=(B𝒊,+−B¯𝒊,−B𝒊,−B¯𝒊,+).\mathcal{B}_{\bm{i}}=\begin{pmatrix}B_{{\bm{i}},+}&-\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},-}\\[2.0pt] B_{{\bm{i}},-}&\phantom{-}\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},+}\end{pmatrix}. (2)

The two components carry opposite emergent gauge charge but equal physical electric charge, and their hopping is governed by the same link field ui​ju_{ij} that defines the spinon ansatz [second relation in Eq. (1)]. Throughout, we hold ui​ju_{ij} fixed at the link field of the undoped state, that is, we assume that the doped carriers do not rearrange the flux pattern of the parent ansatz. Section VII.3 estimates the doping range over which this assumption holds. The square- and triangular-lattice versions of this construction are given in Refs. [18, 31].

On kagome the sign of the chargon hopping relative to ui​ju_{ij} is gauge invariant, and it is fixed by the sign of the electron hopping. The sign amounts to a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} flux per triangle of the chargon hopping. On the bipartite square lattice this flux can be removed by a gauge transformation, and on the triangular lattice it is undone by a point-group operation (Sec. II.3). With the nearest-neighbor spinon correlator of the parent state, ⟨f𝒊​σ†​f𝒋​σ⟩=c1​si​j\langle f^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\sigma}f_{{\bm{j}}\sigma}\rangle=c_{1}s_{ij} with c1=0.221c_{1}=0.221 (Sec. II.3), and ui​j=t​si​j​τ3u_{ij}=t\,s_{ij}\tau^{3} the link field of Eq. (5), the electron hopping −tc∑⟨i​j⟩​σ(c𝒊​σ†c𝒋​σ+H.c.)-t_{c}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle\sigma}(c^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\sigma}c_{{\bm{j}}\sigma}+{\rm H.c.}) decouples on the chargons as

The Cu–O–Cu hopping of herbertsmithite has this sign, which places the flat band at the bottom of the Cu manifold and the Dirac point at n=4/3n=4/3 [90]. In this decoupling the chargon hopping is tB=2​c1​|tc|≃0.44​|tc|t_{B}=2c_{1}|t_{c}|\simeq 0.44\,|t_{c}|.

The physical electron pair operator follows from Eq. (1) by inspection. We replace the spinon bilinears by their mean-field amplitudes.
