A global maximization of ∑rρr3\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3} over the quartic level set of the II- branch selects an unbalanced four-valley state with the closed-form valley weights

nη=14​(1±13),∑rρr3=(2+14​3)/N2,n_{\eta}=\tfrac{1}{4}\Big(1\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\Big),\qquad\textstyle\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3}=\big(2+\tfrac{1}{4\sqrt{3}}\big)\big/N^{2}, (25)

with heavy and light valleys alternating within each translation pair [Fig. 5(c)]. To derive Eq. (25) in closed form, parametrize the II- level set as B=(cos⁡a2,sin⁡a2​ei​α,sin⁡a2​ei⁡(α+γ−π),cos⁡a2​ei​γ)/2B=\big(\cos\tfrac{a}{2},\ \sin\tfrac{a}{2}\,e^{i\alpha},\ \sin\tfrac{a}{2}\,e^{i(\alpha+\gamma-\pi)},\ \cos\tfrac{a}{2}\,e^{i\gamma}\big)/\sqrt{2}, with ∑rρr=1\sum_{r}\rho_{r}=1 throughout this paragraph. The quartic moment is constant on it, N​∑rρr2=43N\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2}=\tfrac{4}{3}, and the sextic moment is N2​∑rρr3=2−38​sin2⁡a​cos⁡a​sin⁡2​α​sin⁡3​γN^{2}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3}=2-\tfrac{3}{8}\,\sin^{2}\!a\,\cos a\,\sin 2\alpha\,\sin 3\gamma. Its global extrema are 2±1/(4​3)2\pm 1/(4\sqrt{3}), attained for example at cosa=±1/3\cos a=\pm 1/\sqrt{3} with α=7​π/4\alpha=7\pi/4 and γ=3​π/2\gamma=3\pi/2, while the two-valley endpoints a=0,πa=0,\pi and the balanced four-valley states sit at 22. The negative-definite sextic that on-site repulsion generates selects the maximum, 2+1/(4​3)=2.14432+1/(4\sqrt{3})=2.1443 at cosa=+1/3\cos a=+1/\sqrt{3}, which is the state of Eq. (25).

That argument maximizes only on the II- level set. At the Hubbard quartic, however, the whole degenerate manifold is flat, including states of intermediate pair population that the level set does not contain. The selection is nevertheless global. To see this, consider the wider family

B=(s​c,s​d​ei​α,−1−s​d​ei⁡(α+γ),1−s​c​ei​γ),B=\big(\sqrt{s}\,c,\ \sqrt{s}\,d\,e^{i\alpha},\ -\sqrt{1-s}\,d\,e^{i(\alpha+\gamma)},\ \sqrt{1-s}\,c\,e^{i\gamma}\big), (26)

with c=cos⁡a2c=\cos\tfrac{a}{2}, d=sin⁡a2d=\sin\tfrac{a}{2} and 0≤s≤10\leq s\leq 1. Its endpoints s=0,1s=0,1 are the phase-I pair sphere, its midpoint s=12s=\tfrac{1}{2} is the level set above, and the projected quartic moment is N​∑rρr2=43N\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2}=\tfrac{4}{3} on all of it. On this family

N2​∑rρr3=2−3​[s⁡(1−s)]3/2​sin2⁡a​cos⁡a​sin⁡2​α​sin⁡3​γ,N^{2}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3}=2-3\,[s(1-s)]^{3/2}\,\sin^{2}\!a\,\cos a\,\sin 2\alpha\,\sin 3\gamma, (27)

and the resolvent element that the sextic ranks is

v†​G​vN=rI+4​s​(1−s)​(r0−rI)+2+63​(N2​∑rρr3−2),\frac{v^{\dagger}Gv}{N}=r_{\rm I}+4s(1-s)\,(r_{0}-r_{\rm I})+\frac{2+\sqrt{6}}{3}\Big(N^{2}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3}-2\Big), (28)

with rI=(12−6)/108r_{\rm I}=(12-\sqrt{6})/108 the phase-I value and r0=(48+23​6)/432r_{0}=(48+23\sqrt{6})/432. Both ss-dependent terms increase with s⁡(1−s)s(1-s), since r0>rIr_{0}>r_{\rm I} and |sin2⁡a​cos⁡a|≤2/(3​3)|\sin^{2}\!a\,\cos a|\leq 2/(3\sqrt{3}), so the maximum over α\alpha and γ\gamma at fixed ss is monotone in s⁡(1−s)s(1-s) and is attained at s=12s=\tfrac{1}{2}. The angular maximum there lies at |cos⁡a|=1/3|\cos a|=1/\sqrt{3} and gives v†​G​v/N=r0+(2+6)/(12​3)=0.4555999v^{\dagger}Gv/N=r_{0}+(2+\sqrt{6})/(12\sqrt{3})=0.4555999, which is the state of Eq. (25). Direct maximization of v†​G​vv^{\dagger}Gv over all four parameters on the 432432-site torus returns the same maximizer (to 4×10−84\times 10^{-8} in ss and cos⁡a\cos a) and the same value. Equations (27) and (28) reproduce the lattice element to 3×10−153\times 10^{-15} over random points of the manifold. The minimum, 2−1/(4​3)2-1/(4\sqrt{3}) at cosa=−1/3\cos a=-1/\sqrt{3}, is what a positive representative sextic +∑rρr3+\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3} would select. It is the density conjugate ρ→2​ρ¯−ρ\rho\to 2\bar{\rho}-\rho of the maximum up to a lattice translation, with the same valley weights (heavy and light valleys interchanged), the same cell, and the same stabilizer. The sextic fixes the sign of the K/2K/2 modulation but not the crystal itself.

In its valley projection, the unconstrained lattice minimization of Sec. VII.1, which contains only on-site UU, returns the valley weights 0.3940.394 and 0.1060.106, i.e. 14​(1±1/3)\tfrac{1}{4}(1\pm 1/\sqrt{3}), and the projected moment N2​∑rρr3=2.1443=2+1/(4​3)N^{2}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3}=2.1443=2+1/(4\sqrt{3}). The moment of the lattice density itself is lower, because the weight outside the four valleys screens the modulation (Sec. VII.1). That minimization realizes the state of Eq. (25), not its conjugate. Its real-space density is a thirty-six-site crystal (twelve primitive cells forming the 12×12\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12} R​30∘R30^{\circ} supercell) with five density levels per cell, ρ/ρ¯=1−1/3\rho/\bar{\rho}=1-1/\sqrt{3}, 1−1/2+1/(2​3)1-1/\sqrt{2}+1/(2\sqrt{3}), 1−1/(2​3)1-1/(2\sqrt{3}), 1+1/31+1/\sqrt{3}, and 1+1/2+1/(2​3)1+1/\sqrt{2}+1/(2\sqrt{3}) (0.42260.4226, 0.58160.5816, 0.71130.7113, 1.57741.5774, and 1.99581.9958), with multiplicities (6,6,12,6,6)(6,6,12,6,6). Its Bragg content separates cleanly. The charge order lives purely on the K/2K/2 star, because the MM-point charge components of the two pairs cancel identically, while the loop currents modulate on the MM and KK stars.

A full group closure within the full 288-element projective symmetry group finds a stabilizer generated by the supercell translations (twelve on the 12×1212\times 12 torus, the lattice of the thirty-six-site cell) together with a magnetic point group of order twelve. That point group consists of the six unitary rotations C6kC_{6}^{k} about a hexagon center and the six mirrors, each present only in combination with Θ\Theta. No unitary mirror and no translation beyond the supercell lattice survives, so the stabilizer is the magnetic point group 6​m′​m′6m^{\prime}m^{\prime} modulo the supercell translations.

Like the phase-I states, the selected state is a magnetic (𝒯\mathcal{T}-breaking, current-carrying) crystal, and its phase degrees of freedom are locked already at sextic order. Unlike the uni-MM stripe, however, it is not protected against a net orbital moment or a polar Kerr response (Sec. IV.2). Its point group 6​m′​m′6m^{\prime}m^{\prime} is a ferromagnetic class, and with three equal current arms the crystal carries the A2′A_{2}^{\prime} composite Δ1′​Δ2′​Δ3′\Delta_{1}^{\prime}\Delta_{2}^{\prime}\Delta_{3}^{\prime}.

The competing representatives are cleanly ranked by the on-site moment N2​∑rρr3N^{2}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3} with ∑rρr=1\sum_{r}\rho_{r}=1, i.e. ⟨ρ3⟩/⟨ρ⟩3\langle\rho^{3}\rangle/\langle\rho\rangle^{3}. The selected state has 2+1/(4​3)=2.14432+1/(4\sqrt{3})=2.1443, while the cross-pair two-valley states and the balanced four-valley states are degenerate at 22. The generic members of the latter are fully chiral, with no antiunitary element in their stabilizer. The sextic moment spreads by 1/(8​3)=7.2%1/(8\sqrt{3})=7.2\% of the competitors’ value [1/(8​3+1)=6.7%1/(8\sqrt{3}+1)=6.7\% of 2.14432.1443]. The derived sextic separates the states more strongly, because on the level set v†​G​vv^{\dagger}Gv is an affine, not a proportional, function of the moment [Eq. (24)]. The selected state has v†​G​v/N=0.4556v^{\dagger}Gv/N=0.4556 against 0.24150.2415 for both competitors. This gives a sextic-energy gain of 4×0.214​U2​x3/t=0.86​U2​x3/t4\times 0.214\,U^{2}x^{3}/t=0.86\,U^{2}x^{3}/t per site, or 89%89\% of the competitors’ sextic energy. Symmetry fixes which anisotropies are allowed, whereas the sign and the competition of the higher-order coefficients are set microscopically, and a sextic of the opposite sign would select the density-conjugate point of the manifold.

The K/2K/2 star has appeared before in the kagome problem. The thirty-six-site valence-bond crystal [89, 114], the classic competitor of the Dirac spin liquid [134, 52], is a 12×12\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12} (R​30∘R30^{\circ}) crystal whose superlattice Bragg vectors have length |K|/2|K|/2 along the KK directions [52]. The sextic-selected chargon crystal of Eq. (25) occupies the same thirty-six-site cell, which no order of the flux sector has. The singlet monopoles of the DSL carry the three MM momenta [116], which generate only the 2×22\times 2 twelve-site superlattice, and every nonzero vector of that superlattice is longer than |K|/2|K|/2. Monopole condensation alone therefore cannot produce a thirty-six-site cell, whereas chargon condensation produces it directly.

The two states are nonetheless sharply different. The VBC preserves time reversal and, in the pinwheel form of Refs. [89, 114], the sixfold rotations but not the mirrors (point group C6C_{6}). Only the variant of Ref. [52] has the full C6​vC_{6v} [53]. The chargon crystal breaks 𝒯\mathcal{T} and retains mirrors only in combination with time reversal, so its symmetry is a magnetic space group on the lattice of the VBC.

That the projected Hubbard functional lies on the I/II boundary may be read as a Landau-theoretic counterpart of the long-standing competition between MM-type and K/2K/2-type orders in kagome numerics. The microscopic interaction is poised between the two stars, and terms beyond the quartic level select the winner, through spin-Peierls energetics for the undoped VBC [52] and through sextic selection and doping commensuration for the chargon crystals (Sec. VII).

IV.4 Order-parameter catalog

Table 2 lists the gauge-invariant particle–hole composites and their quantum numbers. The list is the same for the U(1) state and all four ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants. The momentum-star decomposition of the sixteen bilinears and ten pair composites, and the calibration of the C6​v′′′C_{6v}^{\prime\prime\prime} labels, are given in Appendix H.

Beyond the MM-triplets discussed above, the KK-point composite realizes a 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} loop-current crystal that is C3C_{3}-symmetric (C3C_{3} eigenvalue +1+1) and 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd. It is not a charge order. The site-density form factor at KK vanishes identically for every condensate, and so does the gauge-invariant bond charge at KK out to third-neighbor range, so within the constructions tested the KK star is not a local charge-density or bond-charge channel. It can carry loop current, which makes it a target for probes of orbital magnetism and not for x-ray or electron diffraction (Sec. VIII).

The chargon mechanism produces the enlarged 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} cell without rotational symmetry breaking, but in the current channel. The KK-point CDW of ScV6Sn6, whose three CDW peaks show no C3C_{3} anisotropy (unlike the 2×22\times 2 kagome-metal CDWs [24]), shares this cell and its point symmetry, but not the channel or the (phononic) mechanism.

The Γ\Gamma-point valley polarization Δ​N\Delta N is a staggered (Haldane-like) flux order, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd, C6C_{6}-odd, σv\sigma_{v}-odd and σd\sigma_{d}-even (B2′B_{2}^{\prime}). The same valley-polarization bilinear is a charge stripe on the square lattice [18] and an opposite-flux order on the triangular lattice [31]. Kagome behaves like the triangular case, in that valley imbalance comes with time-reversal breaking.

The F3F_{3} triplet also supports a vestigial composite. Because every element of C6​v′′′C_{6v}^{\prime\prime\prime} acts on the F3F_{3} triplet (Δ1,Δ2,Δ3)(\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2},\Delta_{3}) by a signed permutation of the three MM points, the translation-invariant squares (Δ12,Δ22,Δ32)(\Delta_{1}^{2},\Delta_{2}^{2},\Delta_{3}^{2}) carry the permutation representation A1⊕E2A_{1}\oplus E_{2} (the cross terms Δi​Δj\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j}, i≠ji\neq j, form a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even F1F_{1} MM-triplet). The E2E_{2} doublet 𝒩=(2​Δ12−Δ22−Δ32,3​(Δ22−Δ32))\mathcal{N}=\big(2\Delta_{1}^{2}-\Delta_{2}^{2}-\Delta_{3}^{2},\ \sqrt{3}(\Delta_{2}^{2}-\Delta_{3}^{2})\big) is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even, C2C_{2}-even, translation-invariant ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3} nematic that rotates by 120∘120^{\circ} under C3C_{3}. Because it is quadratic in the triplet, symmetry allows it to order where ⟨Δi⟩=0\langle\Delta_{i}\rangle=0, so a vestigial nematic phase above the MM-triplet transition is permitted. Whether such a phase occurs, and at what temperature, is a question about fluctuations.

To evaluate the nematic on the mean-field condensates, take ∑η|Bη|2=1\sum_{\eta}|B_{\eta}|^{2}=1 and the one-arm normalization |Δ|=12|\Delta|=\tfrac{1}{2} of Appendix H. The uni-MM stripe, with one arm activated, then has |𝒩|=12​ρ¯ 2|\mathcal{N}|=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bar{\rho}^{\,2}, and the three one-arm states give the three nematic directions. The triple-MM state at the body diagonal has 𝒩=0\mathcal{N}=0 (three equal arms, |Δi|=1/(2​3)|\Delta_{i}|=1/(2\sqrt{3})). The K/2K/2 crystal of Eq. (25) has 𝒩=0\mathcal{N}=0 because its F3F_{3} triplet vanishes identically. Its stabilizer contains C2C_{2} about a hexagon center, and F3F_{3} is C2C_{2}-odd. Its particle–hole MM weight resides entirely in the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd current triplet F2′F_{2}^{\prime}, with three equal arms. Only the zeros and the ratios of these values are independent of the normalization. On the pair sphere Δi=ni/2\Delta_{i}=n_{i}/2 in an orthonormal frame, so 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the ℓ=2\ell=2 harmonic of the Bloch vector. The in-pair group Oh\mathrm{O}_{h} (Sec. III.3), whose first anisotropy is ℓ=4\ell=4, excludes this harmonic from the condensate energy, yet it is present as an E2E_{2} order parameter.

The charge and current MM-triplets are locked to each other by symmetry as long as the Γ\Gamma-point flux is ordered. At mean field the locking is automatic, because at each activated MM point the F3F_{3} and F2′F_{2}^{\prime} composites are the two Hermitian parts of a single bilinear of the condensate, activated with equal weight (Sec. IV.2). Beyond mean field the gauge-invariant composites are the physical order parameters, and one may ask whether fluctuations can split the single Higgs transition into separate charge-order and loop-current transitions. Averaging over the full 288-element projective symmetry group shows that the space of invariant trilinears built from one component of Δ​N\Delta N, one of the F3F_{3} triplet and one of the F2′F_{2}^{\prime} triplet is exactly one-dimensional,

ℒ3=Δ​N​∑i=13ϵi​Δi​Δi′,ϵ=(+,−,+),\mathcal{L}_{3}=\Delta N\sum_{i=1}^{3}\epsilon_{i}\,\Delta_{i}\Delta_{i}^{\prime},\qquad\epsilon=(+,-,+), (29)

in the component convention of Appendix H. No invariant of the forms F3​F2′​F2′F_{3}F_{2}^{\prime}F_{2}^{\prime}, F3​F3​F2′F_{3}F_{3}F_{2}^{\prime}, Δ​N​F3​F3\Delta N\,F_{3}F_{3} or Δ​N​F2′​F2′\Delta N\,F_{2}^{\prime}F_{2}^{\prime} exists, and the first coupling that does not involve the flux is quartic (four invariants of the form F3​F3​F2′​F2′F_{3}F_{3}F_{2}^{\prime}F_{2}^{\prime}).

Wherever the B2′B_{2}^{\prime} flux is ordered, Eq. (29) mixes the two triplets linearly, so neither can order without inducing the other, and the MM-point charge order and the loop-current order set in at a single transition. This holds on every phase-I condensate and throughout the upper stage of the two-stage finite-temperature structure of Sec. VIII. Only when the flux is absent and time reversal is restored are the two irreps coupled at quartic order alone, and only then can they order at separate transitions. On every phase-I state ℒ3\mathcal{L}_{3} takes the same value, −14​ρ¯ 3-\tfrac{1}{4}\bar{\rho}^{\,3} in the normalization used for the vestigial nematic above, as the equal-weight activation of Sec. IV.2 implies. On the K/2K/2 crystal the trilinear vanishes, since there Δ​N=0\Delta N=0 and the F3F_{3} triplet vanishes identically.

In the undoped spin liquid, the operator content of the DSL below scaling dimension two (sixteen fermion bilinears and six monopoles) carries only Γ\Gamma- and MM-point momenta, and all its MM-triplets are C2C_{2}-even. The VBS channels (Hastings’ David-star pattern among them) are F1F_{1}, and the three spin-singlet monopoles form F1⊕F2F_{1}\oplus F_{2}, two 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even triplets distinguished by their mirror eigenvalue [45, 116, 118].

Each monopole triplet carries a single time-reversal parity. This follows from 𝒯2=1\mathcal{T}^{2}=1. For an antiunitary 𝒯\mathcal{T} with 𝒯​Φ†​𝒯−1=ei​β​Φ\mathcal{T}\Phi^{\dagger}\mathcal{T}^{-1}=e^{i\beta}\Phi one has β∈{0,π}\beta\in\{0,\pi\}, so the two Hermitian components of a monopole share one parity instead of splitting into an even and an odd part. The argument does not fix which parity is realized, since β=0\beta=0 makes both components even and β=π\beta=\pi makes both odd. We take β=0\beta=0 for the singlet monopoles as an input from the explicit monopole computation of Refs. [118, 116], which identifies the spin-singlet monopoles with 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even valence-bond orders and the spin-triplet monopoles with 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd magnetic orders.

The chargon current triplet F2′F_{2}^{\prime} is the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd partner of the monopole triplet F2F_{2} in the same spatial channel (C2C_{2}-even, both mirrors odd). The two are distinct order parameters, and at the level of masses and monopoles the Higgs (chargon) sector of the doped system and the flux (monopole) sector of the undoped magnet share no channel at all. F2′F_{2}^{\prime} and F3F_{3} do reappear in the parent, among its conserved SU(4) currents at the MM points, whose scaling dimension is exactly two. The chargon composites couple linearly to these currents, while the parent’s masses and monopoles do not enter. The F2′F_{2}^{\prime} channel is also the one selected by the weak-coupling loop-current theory of the kagome metals [34, 138]. The MM-point current order of Ref. [34] transforms as A2A_{2} of the little group C2​vC_{2v} (see its supplementary classification), which is F2′F_{2}^{\prime} in the present labeling. In both works the Landau trilinear vanishes by time reversal, just as every cubic vanishes here.

Among masses and monopoles the F3F_{3} channel is populated by the chargon sector alone. It is also the representation of the classical kagome ground states at the MM points, whose symmetry, as Hermele et al. noted, is absent from every enhanced ASL observable [45]. The “missing” classical MM-point representation thus reappears in the charge sector of the doped system, as a spin singlet and not as a magnetic order.

Because the MM-point fluctuations of the undoped DSL are numerically weak in projected wave functions [45], the orders cataloged here are best regarded as doping induced and new in the symmetry channels they occupy, and not as amplified intrinsic fluctuations of the parent magnet.

V ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants

V.1 The four neighbors of the Dirac spin liquid

Lu, Ran, and Lee [86] classified the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids continuously connected to the [0,π][0,\pi] DSL and found four, which we label α,β,γ,δ\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta. All four share trivial translation dressings and g𝒯=i​τ1g_{\mathcal{T}}=i\tau^{1}, η𝒯=η12=ηC6​T1=−1\eta_{\mathcal{T}}=\eta_{12}=\eta_{C_{6}T_{1}}=-1. They differ only by uniform i​τ3i\tau^{3} dressings of C6C_{6} and/or σ\sigma, that is, by the sign triple (ησ,ησ​C6,ηC6)(\eta_{\sigma},\eta_{\sigma C_{6}},\eta_{C_{6}}). Here ησ​C6\eta_{\sigma C_{6}} is the phase of the projective relation σ−1​C6​σ​C6=e\sigma^{-1}C_{6}\sigma C_{6}=e, gσ†​(C6​(i))​gC6​(C6​(i))​gσ​(i)​gC6​(σ⁡(i))=ησ​C6​τ0g_{\sigma}^{\dagger}(C_{6}(i))\,g_{C_{6}}(C_{6}(i))\,g_{\sigma}(i)\,g_{C_{6}}(\sigma(i))=\eta_{\sigma C_{6}}\tau^{0} [Eq. (A14) of Ref. [86]]. Defining the middle entry through (gσ​gC6)2(g_{\sigma}g_{C_{6}})^{2} instead would multiply it by ησ\eta_{\sigma} and reverse it for γ\gamma and δ\delta. The four triples are

α⁡(No. 6):\displaystyle\alpha\ (\text{No.~6}): (+,−,+),\displaystyle(+,-,+),\qquad β⁡(No. 2):\displaystyle\beta\ (\text{No.~2}): (+,+,−),\displaystyle(+,+,-), (30)
γ⁡(No. 14):\displaystyle\gamma\ (\text{No.~14}): (−,−,+),\displaystyle(-,-,+),\qquad δ⁡(No. 16):\displaystyle\delta\ (\text{No.~16}): (−,+,−),\displaystyle(-,+,-),

in the numbering of Ref. [86]. We have constructed all four explicitly and validated their symmetric pairing content, range by range, against Eqs. (C16)–(C19) of Ref. [86] (twenty independent counts; Table 3). We quote the real-space form factors as the ratio of the pairing amplitude to the hopping amplitude on the same bond, Δi​j/χi​j\Delta_{ij}/\chi_{ij}, which is invariant under the residual ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge transformations of the descendants, whereas the sign of Δi​j\Delta_{ij} on any single bond is not. A uniform U(1) rotation of the parent’s invariant gauge group multiplies the ratio by a global phase, so its overall sign is conventional and only its bond-to-bond pattern is physical.

Symmetry fixes the pattern of this ratio but not its magnitude, which is a free variational parameter. The state α\alpha carries nearest-neighbor pairing with sgn⁡(Δi​j/χi​j)=+1\mathrm{sgn}(\Delta_{ij}/\chi_{ij})=+1 on up-triangles and −1-1 on down-triangles, which is an ff-wave sign structure. The state γ\gamma carries the analogous alternation on the second-neighbor inscribed triangles, and the second-neighbor pairing of β\beta follows the 2NN hopping sign pattern. Each of these patterns is fixed uniquely by symmetry (Appendix F).

Of the four, only β\beta gaps the spinon Dirac cones [86]. For this reason β\beta was originally proposed as the candidate for the fully gapped spin liquid supported by density-matrix renormalization and tensor-network studies [134, 23, 91]. It is also the kagome channel whose Higgs criticality is analyzed in Ref. [30] (Appendix F). Variational calculations found the Dirac state stable against opening the β\beta gap [51], and Lanczos-improved wave functions placed the gapless DSL marginally below it with a vanishing spin gap [54, 56]. Subsequent DMRG work shifted the balance toward the DSL, finding a much smaller spin gap together with Dirac-cone signatures matching the [0,π][0,\pi] ansatz [43], and tensor-network and entanglement studies concur [81, 142]. The α\alpha state has numerical support of its own. A pseudofermion functional-renormalization study of the kagome Heisenberg model, combined with a self-consistent spinon mean field, identified a gapless ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquid of this type [44]. For our purposes the four states enter on an equal footing, as the four symmetry-distinct pairing channels through which the doped DSL can superconduct, whatever the verdict on the undoped system. The classification does not select among them energetically, and we make no claim about which one is realized.

The classification assumes translation-invariant spinon pairing. A recent machine-learning variational study proposes instead that the kagome ground state is a spinon pair-density wave descending from the same [0,π][0,\pi] DSL, with spinon Cooper pairs whose center-of-mass momentum lies at the MM point [143], a finite-momentum ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} class outside Eq. (30). Its variational energies have been challenged as an artifact of non-ergodic Monte Carlo sampling, and ergodic sampling is reported to give energies above the DMRG benchmarks [67]. Independently of these energetics, translations by one lattice constant act as pure gauge transformations because the pair momentum is MM, and the induced composites sit at 2​M≡02M\equiv 0. The projective symmetry analysis that underlies the composite catalog of Sec. IV.4 then shows that the state breaks neither time reversal nor any lattice symmetry.

V.2 Chargon spectra with pairing

In the chargon sector the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} perturbation is strongly constrained. For the β\beta state, the only symmetric Higgs channel at on-site and nearest-neighbor range is the uniform on-site term λ​B†​τ1​B\lambda\,B^{\dagger}\tau^{1}B. The single symmetric NN pattern of β\beta is an invariant-gauge-group rotation of the hopping and is physically trivial, as in the triangular case [31]. The NN pattern of α\alpha, unlike that of β\beta, has zero overlap with the hopping and is the genuine ff-wave pairing of Table 4, which, as shown below, preserves the flat bands. Hereafter Δ2\Delta_{2} denotes the second-neighbor pair amplitude of β\beta, the pairing partner of the second-neighbor hopping χ2\chi_{2} of Sec. II.3 (Appendix F), and no longer the MM-triplet component of Sec. IV.4. The on-site term alone is the case Δ2=0\Delta_{2}=0.

With only the on-site term switched on, the β\beta chargon doublet spectrum takes the closed form

E±​(𝐤)=±t2​m​(𝐤)2+λ2,E_{\pm}(\mathbf{k})=\pm\sqrt{t^{2}m(\mathbf{k})^{2}+\lambda^{2}}, (31)

where m⁡(𝐤)m(\mathbf{k}) are the eigenvalues of the 6×66\times 6 Bloch hopping matrix M⁡(𝐤)M(\mathbf{k}) of Sec. II.2 (unrelated to the MM point of the Brillouin zone). The corresponding 12×1212\times 12 Bloch problem is (H+λ​Λλ​ΛH−)\begin{pmatrix}H_{+}&\lambda\Lambda\\ \lambda\Lambda&H_{-}\end{pmatrix}, where H±H_{\pm} are the Bloch hopping matrices of the two chargon components, H+=−H−H_{+}=-H_{-}, and Λ⁡(𝐤)\Lambda(\mathbf{k}) is that of the pairing pattern. It has the Bogoliubov–de Gennes form in the (B+,B−)(B_{+},B_{-}) isospin space, which produces the E→−EE\to-E symmetry. It nevertheless conserves chargon number and contains no anomalous term, so all twelve bands are physical chargon states. We have verified Eq. (31) on the torus for λ/t=0\lambda/t=0–44 at Δ2=0\Delta_{2}=0. The four valleys remain pinned at 𝐐1​…​4\mathbf{Q}_{1\dots 4} and nondegenerate for all λ\lambda, and the flat pair stays exactly flat at −4​t2+λ2-\sqrt{4t^{2}+\lambda^{2}}. Because the second-neighbor pair form factor does not commute with M⁡(𝐤)M(\mathbf{k}), the β\beta spectrum has no closed form once Δ2\Delta_{2} is switched on. At the valleys the effective pair field combines the on-site and second-neighbor amplitudes as

λeff=λ−2​Δ2,\lambda_{\rm eff}=\lambda-2\Delta_{2}\,, (32)

because the 2NN form factor has valley eigenvalue exactly −2-2 in the flux-canonical sign convention νi​j=−si​k​sk​j\nu_{ij}=-s_{ik}s_{kj} of Sec. II.3 (reversing the overall sign of the form factor requires Δ2→−Δ2\Delta_{2}\to-\Delta_{2}). The corresponding combination at the spinon Dirac points, a different momentum in a different sector, has different weights [(−1:3+1:−(3−1))(-1:\sqrt{3}{+}1:-(\sqrt{3}{-}1)) for (on-site : 2NN : NN), Eq. (C24) of Ref. [86]].

Figure 6 shows the four doublet band structures. The NN ff-wave pairing of α\alpha leaves the chargon flat bands exactly flat at ±2​t\pm 2t for all pairing amplitudes. The line-graph kernel persists in the pairing channel, so the kagome flat-band structure survives both the [0,π][0,\pi] flux and the α\alpha-type Higgs field. With λ\lambda switched on, the condensed B−B_{-} acquires a B+B_{+} admixture. For the on-site term of β\beta its weight is [λ/2​(1+6)​t]2+O⁡(λ4)[\lambda/2(1{+}\sqrt{6})t]^{2}+O(\lambda^{4}), which we have verified numerically at the sub-percent level. A physical pair amplitude linear in λ\lambda also appears. Its leading term, which fixes its symmetry, is the composite of Eq. (33) below. The admixture channel depends on the descendant and is determined by the 6×66\times 6 Bloch block at the valley momentum, where the B+B_{+} spectrum is {−2t(×2),(1−6)t,t(×2),(1+6)t}\{-2t\,(\times 2),\ (1-\sqrt{6})t,\ t\,(\times 2),\ (1+\sqrt{6})t\}, so the admixture statements below hold exactly for the infinite lattice.

Normalize each pattern so that its largest bond amplitude is λ\lambda. Every symmetric pattern of β\beta then acts on the four valley states as a scalar, with eigenvalues of modulus 11, 22 and 6\sqrt{6} for its on-site, second-neighbor and third-neighbor-chain patterns, and maps them onto the top level of the B+B_{+} spectrum at (1+6)​t(1+\sqrt{6})t. The nearest-neighbor pattern is the pure-gauge rotation of the hopping noted above, and the second-neighbor eigenvalue is −2-2 in the flux-canonical convention νi​j=−si​k​sk​j\nu_{ij}=-s_{ik}s_{kj} of Sec. II.3. The admixture goes through the energy denominator 2​(1+6)​t=6.90​t2(1+\sqrt{6})t=6.90\,t, and the on-site weight is [λ/2​(1+6)​t]2=(7−2​6)​λ2/100​t2[\lambda/2(1+\sqrt{6})t]^{2}=(7-2\sqrt{6})\lambda^{2}/100t^{2}.

The patterns of α\alpha (nearest-neighbor and across-hexagon third-neighbor) and of δ\delta (third-neighbor chain) instead map each valley state entirely onto the fourfold B+B_{+} level at (1−6)​t(1-\sqrt{6})t. That level is the partner of the valley level. The dispersive B−B_{-} spectrum has the exact symmetry E→−2​t−EE\to-2t-E. It follows from the line-graph structure of Sec. II.3, because the honeycomb bands ϵa​(𝐤)\epsilon_{a}(\mathbf{k}) are symmetric under ϵ→−ϵ\epsilon\to-\epsilon. The valley at −(1+6)​t-(1+\sqrt{6})t has a partner at (6−1)​t(\sqrt{6}-1)t at the same momentum, and the B+B_{+} sector, whose spectrum is the negative of the B−B_{-} spectrum, carries this partner at (1−6)​t(1-\sqrt{6})t. The α\alpha and δ\delta admixtures go through an energy denominator of 2​t2t, with B+B_{+} weights 3​λ2/4​t23\lambda^{2}/4t^{2} (α\alpha) and 3​λ2/2​t23\lambda^{2}/2t^{2} (δ\delta), larger than the on-site weight of β\beta by the factors 3​(1+6)2=35.73(1+\sqrt{6})^{2}=35.7 and 6​(1+6)2=71.46(1+\sqrt{6})^{2}=71.4 (amplitude ratios 5.975.97 and 8.458.45).

For the nearest-neighbor pattern of α\alpha the mapping follows from an algebraic identity. The pattern is B~†​Ξ​B~\tilde{B}^{\dagger}\Xi\tilde{B}, with B~\tilde{B} the signed 4×64\times 6 incidence matrix of Sec. II.3 and Ξ=±1\Xi=\pm 1 on the two sublattices of the honeycomb of triangle centers. It anticommutes with 1−M1-M and squares to 9−(M−1)29-(M-1)^{2}, which equals 33 on the valleys, so it maps each valley state, with squared norm 33, onto its partner. The flat multiplet at Δflat\Delta_{\rm flat} receives no weight from any pattern.

Because the pairing maps each valley onto a single eigenvector and back, the coupled problem closes on a two-level block per valley, and the condensate energy has a closed form. It is −6​t−t2+3​λ2-\sqrt{6}\,t-\sqrt{t^{2}+3\lambda^{2}} for α\alpha and −6​t−t2+6​λ2-\sqrt{6}\,t-\sqrt{t^{2}+6\lambda^{2}} for δ\delta, compared with −(1+6)2​t2+λ2-\sqrt{(1+\sqrt{6})^{2}t^{2}+\lambda^{2}} for the on-site term of β\beta [Eq. (31)]. These values reproduce the exact diagonalization of the paired chargon Hamiltonian on the 12×1212\times 12 torus to 10−1410^{-14}. For the on-site term of β\beta the four valleys remain the nondegenerate minimum of the paired one-body problem for all λ\lambda. For the nearest-neighbor pattern of α\alpha they remain so for λ<0.85​t\lambda<0.85\,t [in closed form λc=t​(3+33)/12\lambda_{c}=t\sqrt{(3+\sqrt{33})/12}, beyond which the minimum moves away from the valleys continuously], and for δ\delta for λ<0.32​t\lambda<0.32\,t. Beyond that value the δ\delta band minimum jumps onto six degenerate points of the magnetic Brillouin zone, Γ\Gamma, YY, SS, (12,0)(\tfrac{1}{2},0) and (0,±14)(0,\pm\tfrac{1}{4}). These fall into three classes under the projective translations [Γ∼Y\Gamma\sim Y, (12,0)∼S(\tfrac{1}{2},0)\sim S and (0,14)∼(0,−14)(0,\tfrac{1}{4})\sim(0,-\tfrac{1}{4})] and all lie on the lines Γ\Gamma–YY–SS of Fig. 2(c) and Γ\Gamma–(12,0)(\tfrac{1}{2},0), along which the lowest band is dispersionless at λ=0\lambda=0. The δ\delta panel of Fig. 6, drawn at 0.4​t0.4\,t, lies beyond this point, and there the lowest band at SS, YY and Γ\Gamma lies below the valley.

For the γ\gamma state the unique symmetric second-neighbor pattern annihilates the four valley states and their partners at (6−1)​t(\sqrt{6}-1)t, though not the rest of the lowest band. The kernel of the pattern is a doubly degenerate flat zero band. The valley state therefore remains an exact eigenvector of the paired one-body Hamiltonian at −(1+6)​t-(1+\sqrt{6})t, and it is the band minimum for λ<0.56​t\lambda<0.56\,t. No B+B_{+} admixture is generated at any order in λ\lambda. The annihilation does not remove the uniform pair channel of γ\gamma. On a condensate with a uniform pair component (Sec. V.3) the composite of Eq. (33) retains a nonzero q=0q=0 component transforming as B2B_{2}. Only its bond-summed (A1A_{1}) part vanishes, as it does for α\alpha (B1B_{1}) and δ\delta (A2A_{2}). The second route to a physical pair amplitude, through the B¯+​B¯−\bar{B}_{+}\bar{B}_{-} term of Eq. (4), which the other three descendants possess (Sec. V.3), is absent for γ\gamma. This protection holds only for the pure valley condensate. On-site repulsion admixes non-condensing states (Sec. IV.1), which the pattern does not annihilate, so an admixture of order U​λU\lambda appears in a density-modulated condensate.

Compare the square-lattice formula for the induced electron pairing [Eq. (3.7) of Ref. [14]]. Its cross term is the product of the two chargon components times the spinon hopping. The kagome theory realizes the limit in which this term vanishes on the DSL condensate itself, because ⟨B+⟩=0\langle B_{+}\rangle=0 at λ=0\lambda=0. It returns only through the λ\lambda-induced B+B_{+} admixture, via the B¯+​B¯−\bar{B}_{+}\bar{B}_{-} term of Eq. (4), which multiplies the spinon hopping and is absent for γ\gamma (Sec. V.3). Every channel is then linear in the spinon pairing, so superconductivity here requires a paired ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} parent and does not follow automatically from confinement.

V.3 Pairing-symmetry map and pair-density waves

Table 4 lists the superconducting channels of the four descendants in terms of the physical electron pair operator. Equation (1) gives c𝒊↑​c𝒋↓=−B¯𝒊,−​B¯𝒋,−​f𝒊↓†​f𝒋↑†+⋯c_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}c_{{\bm{j}}\downarrow}=-\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},-}\bar{B}_{{\bm{j}},-}f^{\dagger}_{{\bm{i}}\downarrow}f^{\dagger}_{{\bm{j}}\uparrow}+\cdots. The omitted terms are proportional either to B¯+​B¯+\bar{B}_{+}\bar{B}_{+} times the spinon pair operator, where the product B¯+​B¯+\bar{B}_{+}\bar{B}_{+} is of second order in λ\lambda, or to B¯±​B¯∓\bar{B}_{\pm}\bar{B}_{\mp} times the spinon hopping. The latter is fed by the B+B_{+} admixture of Sec. V.2 at the same order in λ\lambda as the displayed term. Its amplitude relative to the displayed term is of the order of the admixture amplitude |B+|/|B−||B_{+}|/|B_{-}| divided by the pairing-to-hopping ratio λ/t\lambda/t of the strongest pairing bond. This quotient, the admixture amplitude per unit λ/t\lambda/t, is (6−1)/10=0.145(\sqrt{6}-1)/10=0.145 for the on-site channel of β\beta, 3/2=0.87\sqrt{3}/2=0.87 for α\alpha, 6/2=1.22\sqrt{6}/2=1.22 for δ\delta and zero for γ\gamma. The hopping term carries the same Γ\Gamma-point irreducible representation as the displayed term (A1A_{1} for β\beta and B1B_{1} for α\alpha, while for δ\delta its uniform part vanishes identically because the A2A_{2} irrep is forbidden on nearest-neighbor bonds). The channel assignments below are unaffected, although the term is small only for β\beta. With only B−B_{-} condensed, the electron pair amplitude that carries the classification in a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendant is therefore

Δi​jel=−B¯𝒊,−​B¯𝒋,−​(Δi​jsp)∗,\Delta^{\rm el}_{ij}=-\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},-}\bar{B}_{{\bm{j}},-}\,\big(\Delta^{\rm sp}_{ij}\big)^{*}, (33)

the symmetric chargon pair composite times the conjugate spinon pair amplitude Δi​jsp=⟨f𝒊↑​f𝒋↓⟩\Delta^{\rm sp}_{ij}=\langle f_{{\bm{i}}\uparrow}f_{{\bm{j}}\downarrow}\rangle. Because the spinon pairing of all four descendants is translation invariant, the electron pair momenta are those of the chargon composites. The ten symmetric composites Bη​Bη′B_{\eta}B_{\eta^{\prime}} decompose into Γ\Gamma (×1\times 1), the MM star (×3\times 3) and the K/2K/2 star (×6\times 6), and the uniform member is (B1​B3+B2​B4)/2(B_{1}B_{3}+B_{2}B_{4})/\sqrt{2} (Appendix H). Equation (33) is gauge invariant and transforms under the space group by pure lattice permutation. On the space spanned by the ten composites times the descendant’s projective-symmetry-invariant spinon form factor, its action coincides with the chargon pair representation dressed by the signs that the form factor acquires under C6C_{6} and σ\sigma. The uniform (Γ\Gamma) channel is at most one-dimensional, so the uniform pair channel of each descendant is a one-dimensional irrep. The state β\beta pairs in A1A_{1} (extended ss), α\alpha in B1B_{1} (ff-wave), γ\gamma in B2B_{2} (the second ff-wave), and δ\delta in A2A_{2}, so no chiral d±i​dd\pm id channel appears at this order.

We have verified this exclusion, which follows from symmetry and involves no energetics, on the 12×1212\times 12 torus for every symmetry-allowed spinon form factor of the four descendants through third neighbors. The Γ\Gamma sector transforms as A1A_{1} (β\beta), B1B_{1} (α\alpha), A2A_{2} (δ\delta) and B2B_{2} (γ\gamma), the MM triplet as F3F_{3}, F1F_{1}, F4F_{4} and F2F_{2}, and the E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} multiplicities at Γ\Gamma vanish in every case. At mean field, and at the level of the composite of Eq. (33), which is bilinear in the valley amplitudes, no descendant of the kagome DSL can therefore produce a two-component (E2E_{2}) uniform pair order parameter, and so no d+i​dd+id state.

For the MM-star condensates of phase I the statement holds beyond the bilinear level, at every order in the condensate. A translation pair carries the crystal momenta 𝐐1\mathbf{Q}_{1} and 𝐐1+𝐆2/2\mathbf{Q}_{1}+\mathbf{G}_{2}/2 [Eq. (6)], so every uniform charge-2​e2e composite B¯p​Bq\bar{B}^{\,p}B^{\,q} with p−q=2p-q=2 built from it carries momentum −2​𝐐1-2\mathbf{Q}_{1} modulo 𝐆2/2\mathbf{G}_{2}/2, whose first fractional coordinate is −1/3-1/3. Since this is never a reciprocal-lattice vector, the composite vanishes identically.

On the II- branch the statement holds only at bilinear order. The next composites have bidegree (3,1)(3,1), a pair times a density, and contain a uniform doublet whose Γ\Gamma sector is six-dimensional. It decomposes as A1+B2+E1+E2A_{1}+B_{2}+E_{1}+E_{2} undressed (A2+B1+E1+E2A_{2}+B_{1}+E_{1}+E_{2} for the α\alpha and δ\delta dressings). On the K/2K/2 crystal of Eq. (25) the crystal’s stabilizer, a sixfold rotation combined with a translation, forces the induced uniform composite to be a C6C_{6} eigenvector with chiral eigenvalue. It transforms as E2E_{2} for the descendants α\alpha and γ\gamma, whose form factors are odd under C6C_{6}, and as E1E_{1} for β\beta and δ\delta.

The pair-times-density composite has the form of the standard coupling of intertwined-order Landau theory, in which a pair-density wave times a charge density wave induces a uniform pair component. Here the coupling arises through the feedback of the condensate on the spinon pairing, and its coefficient is dynamical and of relative order xx. On the K/2K/2 branch a small chiral d±i​dd\pm id-like admixture is therefore allowed for α\alpha and γ\gamma, and the exclusion there is a leading-order statement. In the α\alpha state the B1B_{1} uniform amplitude is carried by the nearest-neighbor form factor. It vanishes identically on the across-hexagon third-neighbor form factor, since B1B_{1} is odd under the C2C_{2} that exchanges the two ends of such a bond.

The frequently proposed kagome d+i​dd+id state is thus ruled out for every descendant of the DSL at leading order, and at any order on the MM-star condensates. On the triangular lattice, by contrast, uniform d±i​dd\pm id is allowed by symmetry and is not selected energetically [31].

Other approaches give the same channel structure near 1/31/3 doping. Weak-coupling functional renormalization at the Dirac filling finds a B1​uB_{1u} ff-wave leader with a B2​uB_{2u} alternative [90], and the same B1​uB_{1u}/B2​uB_{2u} pair leads in a random-phase-approximation study of AAV3Sb5 at its van Hove filling [129]. Strong-coupling tensor-network calculations find that the surviving pairing is the Q=0Q=0, sign-alternating nearest-neighbor structure of our α\alpha channel, and that d+i​dd+id is never the ground state [133]. These are dynamical calculations, whereas the present projective classification is a symmetry constraint that forbids a uniform d+i​dd+id at the level of Eq. (33) without ranking the allowed channels. The fRG ff-wave of Ref. [90] is a spin triplet and the parton channels here are classified as singlets, so the agreement with it concerns the spatial form factor only.

A Landau theory of three-component pair-density waves on the kagome lattice and of their charge-6​e6e vestigial phase is developed in Ref. [83]. The MM-point pair triplets of the four descendants realize all four three-dimensional irreps of the extended point group (α→F1\alpha\to F_{1}, γ→F2\gamma\to F_{2}, β→F3\beta\to F_{3}, δ→F4\delta\to F_{4}), in one-to-one correspondence with the dressing table (30). The states β\beta and δ\delta carry odd-parity (C2C_{2}-odd) MM-PDWs. The K/2K/2 pair sextet carries a mirror parity that likewise distinguishes the states (Table 4). The uniform pair component of the selected condensates is fixed branch by branch by the exact identity following Eq. (21), in which the uniform composite (B1​B3+B2​B4)/2(B_{1}B_{3}+B_{2}B_{4})/\sqrt{2} enters. On the unit sphere |B1​B3+B2​B4|=12​[(∑ηnη)2−(𝒫−2​𝒳)]1/2|B_{1}B_{3}+B_{2}B_{4}|=\tfrac{1}{2}\big[(\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta})^{2}-(\mathcal{P}-2\mathcal{X})\big]^{1/2}. It vanishes identically on all of phase I and branch II-, and it reaches its maximum value 12\tfrac{1}{2} only at the II+ vertex (𝒫,𝒳)=(12,+14)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{X})=(\tfrac{1}{2},+\tfrac{1}{4}), represented by the translation-symmetric pair condensate (c1,0,c3,0)(c_{1},0,c_{3},0). On the phase-I and II- arcs this condensate is never selected, and at the projected on-site and nearest-neighbor directions θU\theta_{U} and θV\theta_{V} it is the global maximum of the potential. The condensates selected there carry zero uniform pair component. Phase-I condensates produce pure K/2K/2 pair-density waves, and II- condensates produce K/2K/2 plus MM PDWs. On the II+ arc, θ/π∈(1, 1.63386)\theta/\pi\in(1,\,1.63386), which covers 31.7%31.7\% of the one-angle phase diagram of Fig. 3, the same condensate (c1,0,c3,0)(c_{1},0,c_{3},0) is instead a global minimum. The selected states there carry the full uniform pair component, |B1​B3+B2​B4|=12|B_{1}B_{3}+B_{2}B_{4}|=\tfrac{1}{2}, in addition to their finite-momentum pair content.

On phase I and branch II- the superconductor descending from the kagome DSL is a pair-density wave in the intertwined-order sense [1, 32], with no uniform Josephson component at leading order. The same conclusion was reached for kagome metals in a large-VV patch model at intermediate coupling, in which sublattice interference renders the on-site repulsion irrelevant [130]. Here it holds exactly on the condensate manifold of those two branches. On the triangular lattice, finite-momentum pairing is selected energetically while uniform pairing remains allowed [31]. On kagome the uniform channel is orthogonal at the quartic level to the condensates selected on phase I and branch II-, and it appears only on the II+ arc.

The lowest-order uniform pair composite that the finite-momentum content generates depends on the condensate and follows from the momenta of Table 2. On the II- crystal the three MM components close at second order (2​M≡02M\equiv 0) and the six K/2K/2 components form three (+Q,−Q)(+Q,-Q) mates, all nonzero, so ΔQ​Δ−Q\Delta_{Q}\Delta_{-Q} is a uniform charge-4​e4e composite at second order. On the phase-I sphere the −Q-Q arms vanish identically, so only one member of each mate is nonzero and no charge-4​e4e composite is generated at second order. The triple-MM orbit carries a C3C_{3} triple of K/2K/2 components with Q1+Q2+Q3=0Q_{1}+Q_{2}+Q_{3}=0, whose product is a uniform charge-6​e6e composite at third order. This channel coincides with the vestigial order identified in Ref. [83]. The octic-selected uni-MM stripe carries two K/2K/2 components differing by an MM vector, which close only at sixth order (charge 12​e12e).

Phase-sensitive tunneling on KV3Sb5, read through a Ginzburg–Landau analysis of its doping dependence, supports a sign-changing pair-density wave at the full 2×22\times 2 MM star that is primary, not induced [135]. Nonmagnetic pair-breaking suppresses the pair modulation while the charge order persists and the uniform component strengthens, which is the opposite of an induced-PDW response. The accompanying analysis classifies PDW order parameters by irreps of the same extended point group C6​v′′′C_{6v}^{\prime\prime\prime} used here, and Table 4 gives the complete F1F_{1}–F4F_{4} assignment.

Because KV3Sb5 retains a large uniform pair component [135], the chargon-descendant prediction of no uniform charge-2​e2e component at the quartic level is not tested there, and the data in fact argue against it. The agreement concerns only the irrep classification of the MM-star PDW.

The vortex- and edge-spectroscopy signatures computed for candidate kagome pairings [25] indicate what to look for, channel by channel. The states α\alpha and γ\gamma correspond to the six-pointed-star vortex states and orientation-selective flat Andreev edge bands of the two ff-waves, and β\beta to the featureless Caroli–de Gennes–Matricon ladder of extended ss. The chiral-dd signatures (gapped vortex core, Chern number two) belong to a channel that is absent from the MM-star condensates at any order and induced only at relative order xx on the K/2K/2 branch, for α\alpha and γ\gamma (Sec. V.3).

The correspondence is between pairing channels. The spectra themselves do not carry over, because those calculations assume uniform pairing and the condensates selected here are pair-density waves. Their Bogoliubov–de Gennes problem couples 𝐤\mathbf{k} to −𝐤+𝐐-\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{Q} in a folded zone, so their vortex and edge spectra depend on the modulation components, the normal dispersion and the magnetic symmetries, and we do not compute them here.

VI Chiral descendant

VI.1 Ansatz and identification

The chiral neighbor of the DSL is the Kalmeyer–Laughlin chiral spin liquid stabilized by further-neighbor or explicitly chiral couplings [66, 36, 5, 141, 128, 47]. Its parton ansatz is the oriented flux family of Hu et al. [47],

[θ△,θ⎔;θa​b​c,θa​c​d]=[3​φ1,π−6​φ1;π−2​φ1−φ2, 3​φ2],[\theta_{\triangle},\theta_{\hexagon};\theta_{abc},\theta_{acd}]=[3\varphi_{1},\ \pi-6\varphi_{1};\ \pi-2\varphi_{1}-\varphi_{2},\ 3\varphi_{2}], (34)

with nearest- and second-neighbor hoppings t1​ei​φ1t_{1}e^{i\varphi_{1}}, t2​ei​φ2t_{2}e^{i\varphi_{2}} (the site labels a,b,c,da,b,c,d, the orientation conventions of φ1\varphi_{1} and φ2\varphi_{2} and the second-neighbor sign pattern νi​j\nu_{ij} are defined in Appendix G). The U(1) DSL is the point [0,π;π,0][0,\pi;\pi,0].

We have verified that this state is the chiral spin liquid “CSL C” of the Bieri–Lhuillier–Messio classification [No. 10 of Table VIII in Ref. [7]; No. 15 of Table I in Ref. [8]]. It carries the Kalmeyer–Laughlin projective class (τσ,τR)=(1,0)(\tau_{\sigma},\tau_{R})=(1,0), the only class that admits a nonzero spinon Chern number [7]. Our torus implementation reproduces all four gauge-invariant fluxes of Eq. (34), including the mixed-triangle flux θa​b​c\theta_{abc}, which fixes the otherwise arbitrary global sign of the second-neighbor pattern (Appendix G).

Symmetry also admits a purely imaginary diagonal (intra-hexagon) hopping. The constraint relating a directed bond to its reverse is antilinear, and its solution locks the diagonal phase to βd=π/2\beta_{d}=\pi/2, as tabulated in Ref. [7]. In the time-reversal-symmetric DSL the same bond is forbidden outright, so βd\beta_{d} is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-breaking order-parameter direction and cannot be tuned freely. With nearest-neighbor hopping only, the family reduces to the uniform-flux ansatz [θ,π−2​θ][\theta,\pi-2\theta] of Marston and Zeng [89] and Hastings [41]. In the monopole language the CSL is the DSL with the Γ\Gamma-point singlet mass condensed, and the resulting Chern–Simons term suppresses monopole proliferation [118].

VI.2 Chargon sectors: the two-valley theory and its boundary

The chiral chargon problem has a sector structure with no triangular analog (Fig. 7). Consider first the nearest-neighbor-only point [π/2,0][\pi/2,0] (φ1=π/6\varphi_{1}=\pi/6, t2=0t_{2}=0). It was historically the first kagome CSL candidate, favored at mean field but losing to the DSL after projection [105]. At this point the two chargon sectors are exactly degenerate. The B+B_{+} and B−B_{-} hoppings are the two diagonal entries of ui​ju_{ij} [Eq. (1)], ti​jt_{ij} and −ti​j∗-t_{ij}^{*} (Sec. II.1), so the B−B_{-} hopping is minus the complex conjugate of the B+B_{+} hopping. The sign reversal shifts the flux of every odd loop by π\pi (Sec. II.3) and the conjugation reverses every flux, so B−B_{-} sees the fluxes [π−3​φ1, 6​φ1−π][\pi-3\varphi_{1},\,6\varphi_{1}-\pi], which is the same nearest-neighbor family at φ1→π/3−φ1\varphi_{1}\to\pi/3-\varphi_{1}. At φ1=π/6\varphi_{1}=\pi/6 these coincide with the B+B_{+} fluxes [π/2,0][\pi/2,0]. The two sectors are then U(1) gauge copies of one another (we construct the gauge transformation explicitly on the torus, Appendix G). They have identical spectra and band Chern numbers, band bottoms at −3.045474876​t1-3.045474876\,t_{1}, and four valleys each at 𝐐1​…​4\mathbf{Q}_{1\dots 4}. The NN-only Kalmeyer–Laughlin point is a 4+44{+}4-valley theory of a single chirality and has no two-valley description. (At mean field the [π/2,0][\pi/2,0] ansatz itself has gapped Chern bands [128].)

Moving φ1\varphi_{1} away from π/6\pi/6 splits the sectors, by 1.00​t11.00\,t_{1} at Hu’s φ1=0.0567​π\varphi_{1}=0.0567\pi with t2=0t_{2}=0 [Fig. 7(a)]. Second-neighbor hopping then drives them to cross. At Hu’s optimized phases (φ1,φ2)=(0.0567​π,−0.2807​π)(\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2})=(0.0567\pi,-0.2807\pi) the global chargon minimum switches from the four-valley B−B_{-} sector to the B+B_{+} sector at

r2,c≡|t2/t1|c=0.265082​…,r_{2,c}\equiv|t_{2}/t_{1}|_{c}=0.265082\ldots, (35)

beyond which the B+B_{+} bottom has two nondegenerate valleys [Fig. 7(b)]. Their separation, a gauge-invariant quantity, equals the spinon internode vector (an MM vector), and in the gauge of Appendix A they sit at the spinon Dirac momenta. (On the square lattice chargon minima and spinon nodes coincide automatically [9]. On the kagome DSL they do not, and the coincidence reappears only in the chiral regime.)

With B+B_{+} condensed instead of B−B_{-}, the bookkeeping of Sec. II.1 is mirrored. Equation (1) gives c𝒊​σ=B¯𝒊,+​f𝒊​σc_{{\bm{i}}\sigma}=\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},+}f_{{\bm{i}}\sigma}, so the electron is the spinon itself, not its particle–hole conjugate. The unbroken diagonal charge is QEM+QgQ_{\rm EM}+Q_{g}, under which B+B_{+} is neutral and B−B_{-} carries charge 22. The charge-2​e2e object is again the gauge-neutral composite ⟨B+​B−⟩\langle B_{+}B_{-}\rangle, which now reduces to B−​⟨B+⟩B_{-}\langle B_{+}\rangle and vanishes as long as B−B_{-} stays gapped. In the emergent Gauss law (nf−1)+n+−n−=0(n_{f}-1)+n_{+}-n_{-}=0 (Sec. II.1) the condensate enters with the opposite sign. A B+B_{+} condensate of density xx gives the spinon filling nf=1−xn_{f}=1-x for hole doping and 1+x1+x for electron doping, which is the electron density itself, since the electron is now the spinon. The no-superconductivity argument of Sec. II.3 carries over with the roles of the two sectors exchanged.

Hu et al. provide optimized phases at the coupling point (J2,J3)=(0.5,0.6)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.5,0.6) of their J1J_{1}–J2J_{2}–J3J_{3} model (in units of J1J_{1}), and their quoted mean-field gap can be inverted against our bands. That gap is ≃0.6\simeq 0.6 at the optimum in their normalization Re​t1=1\mathrm{Re}\,t_{1}=1, or 0.6cosφ1=0.5910.6\cos\varphi_{1}=0.591 in units of |t1||t_{1}|. It is a 16×16×316\times 16\times 3-cluster value, which we take as the bulk gap (grid-resolved readings give larger values, Appendix G). Inverting it yields a spinon ratio r2∗≃0.334r_{2}^{*}\simeq 0.334, which lies beyond r2,cr_{2,c}.

Using this value as the chargon ratio assumes that the chargon second-neighbor amplitude is proportional to the spinon variational one, although the two are distinct. The chargon hopping is ti​jelectron​⟨fi†​fj⟩t^{\rm electron}_{ij}\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f_{j}\rangle (Sec. II.1), so an electron model with nearest-neighbor hopping alone gives the chargon no second-neighbor amplitude, however large the spinon ξ2\xi_{2}. The doped state then lies below the crossing, in the four-valley regime.

The variational optimum of Ref. [7] for the same state is |ξ2/ξ1|=0.25/0.75≃0.33|\xi_{2}/\xi_{1}|=0.25/0.75\simeq 0.33 at (J1,J2,Jd)≃(0.63,0.13,0.24)(J_{1},J_{2},J_{d})\simeq(0.63,0.13,0.24), that is, J2/J1≃0.21J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.21 and Jd/J1≃0.38J_{d}/J_{1}\simeq 0.38, where JdJ_{d} is the hexagon-diagonal coupling that Hu et al. call J3J_{3}. This optimum confirms the magnitude of the second-neighbor amplitude but not the regime. Its phases, (φ1,φ2)≃(0.08​π,−0.61​π)(\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2})\simeq(0.08\pi,-0.61\pi) in the conventions fixed by the θa​b​c\theta_{abc} flux, coincide with the (J2,J3)=(0.2,0.4)(J_{2},J_{3})=(0.2,0.4) optimum of Hu et al., (0.0869​π,−0.6150​π)(0.0869\pi,-0.6150\pi). At these phases the sectors do not cross. The four-valley B−B_{-} sector condenses for all r2≤0.4r_{2}\leq 0.4 (margin 0.28​t10.28\,t_{1} at r2=1/3r_{2}=1/3), and a two-valley B−B_{-} sector condenses beyond. The same holds at the other tabulated optima of Ref. [47]. At r2=1/3r_{2}=1/3 the B−B_{-} sector condenses at (0.5,0.7)(0.5,0.7) (four valleys, margin 0.09​t10.09\,t_{1}) and at (0.2,0.3)(0.2,0.3) (two valleys at the Dirac momenta, margin 0.29​t10.29\,t_{1}).

Granting the proportionality of chargon and spinon amplitudes, and within the nearest- and second-neighbor model at the (0.5,0.6)(0.5,0.6) optimum of Hu et al., the doped Kalmeyer–Laughlin state would therefore be a two-valley B+B_{+} chargon theory. We use the representative value r2=0.35r_{2}=0.35 [bottom −3.308​t1-3.308\,t_{1}] for it. The optimized φ2\varphi_{2} varies by a factor of two across the chiral phase, however, and at the other tabulated optima, including Bieri’s point, the doped state condenses the B−B_{-} sector instead, with four or two valleys as listed above. We leave that regime aside.

Below the crossing the condensing sector is the four-valley B−B_{-} sector. A scan of r2r_{2} from 00 to 0.2650.265 in steps of 0.010.01 at Hu’s phases, refined near r2,cr_{2,c}, shows that its minima stay at the valleys 𝐐1​…​4\mathbf{Q}_{1\dots 4} of Eq. (6), as they do at the crossing itself. The four-valley construction of Secs. III and IV applies to this sector once the projective symmetry group is replaced by that of the chiral ansatz, in which time reversal and the mirror survive only in the combination σ​Θ\sigma\Theta, and once the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} pairing channels of Sec. V are dropped, since the pure hopping ansatz lacks them. The Landau invariants of that four-valley chiral theory would have to be rederived.

The crossing is a coincidence of two band bottoms at commensurate momenta, the B+B_{+} pair at the spinon Dirac points (12,14)(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{4}) and (12,34)(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{3}{4}) in units of the magnetic reciprocal vectors 𝐆1,2\mathbf{G}_{1,2} and the B−B_{-} quartet at the valleys 𝐐1​…​4\mathbf{Q}_{1\dots 4} of Eq. (6), so it is grid independent. Bisection on kk grids of Ng=12N_{g}=12, 2424, 4848, 9696 and 192192 points per magnetic reciprocal vector returns the same value r2,c=0.2650822340r_{2,c}=0.2650822340 on every grid, and a continuum refinement of both bottoms agrees to 10−1010^{-10}.

Because the phases are Hu’s quoted optimum, the variations below measure parameter sensitivity and are not an uncertainty estimate. Scaling φ1\varphi_{1} or φ2\varphi_{2} separately by ±10%\pm 10\% moves r2,cr_{2,c} within [0.255, 0.278][0.255,\,0.278], with ∂r2,c/∂ln⁡φ1=−0.105\partial r_{2,c}/\partial\ln\varphi_{1}=-0.105 and ∂r2,c/∂ln⁡φ2=+0.115\partial r_{2,c}/\partial\ln\varphi_{2}=+0.115. The two nearly cancel under a common rescaling. Only a +20%+20\% change in φ2\varphi_{2} pushes the crossing to 0.3370.337, marginally above r2∗r_{2}^{*}. At r2=0.35r_{2}=0.35 the B+B_{+} sector remains the condensing sector under every one of these variations, with a sector margin of 0.174​t10.174\,t_{1} at Hu’s phases. These variations are small compared with the spread of the optimized phases across the chiral phase of Ref. [47] (φ2\varphi_{2} from −0.28​π-0.28\pi to −0.62​π-0.62\pi over the four tabulated optima), over which the condensing sector at r2=1/3r_{2}=1/3 changes as stated above.

These variations stay within the nearest- and second-neighbor model. The crossing is far more sensitive to the purely imaginary intra-hexagon hopping that symmetry also permits (Sec. II.2), whose phase is locked at βd=π/2\beta_{d}=\pi/2. We write its amplitude as the signed coefficient rd=td/t1r_{d}=t_{d}/t_{1} of that pattern. The pattern is fixed by the realified symmetry constraint, whose solution is one dimensional and unimodular with bond phases ±π/2\pm\pi/2 (Appendix G). At r2∗=0.334r_{2}^{*}=0.334 the sector margin is 0.155​t10.155\,t_{1} for rd=0r_{d}=0. It is linear in rdr_{d} and vanishes at rd=+0.0388r_{d}=+0.0388, while the opposite sign enlarges it beyond |rd|=0.4|r_{d}|=0.4. The diagonal link is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd direction in a state that already breaks 𝒯\mathcal{T}, so it is generated, not tuned, and its sign is not free. The half-filled spinon energy responds linearly at rd=0r_{d}=0 and, at every r2r_{2} we have examined, decreases in the direction that closes the margin. Its magnitude follows from the same decoupling, rd=(Jd/J1)​(cd/c1)r_{d}=(J_{d}/J_{1})(c_{d}/c_{1}), where cdc_{d} and c1c_{1} are the projections of ⟨fi†​fj⟩\langle f^{\dagger}_{i}f_{j}\rangle on the diagonal and nearest-neighbor patterns. At r2∗r_{2}^{*} this gives |cd/c1|=0.200|c_{d}/c_{1}|=0.200. Iterated to a fixed point, it gives rd=0.048r_{d}=0.048, 0.1070.107 and 0.2070.207 for Jd/J1=0.20J_{d}/J_{1}=0.20, 0.380.38 and 0.600.60, the last being the J3J_{3} of Hu’s own optimum. All three exceed 0.03880.0388.

Together with the distinction between chargon and spinon links made above, this leaves the two-valley placement without support. If the chargon links are proportional to the spinon links, the same proportionality carries the diagonal link, which closes the sector margin. If they are not, then in an electron model with nearest-neighbor hopping alone the chargon acquires neither a second-neighbor nor a diagonal amplitude, and the state lies below the crossing. We therefore do not claim that the doped chiral state realizes the two-valley regime, although our analysis does not exclude it. Our estimate is unprojected mean field, whereas Hu’s is projected and variational, and the threshold is computed at fixed r2r_{2}, whereas a complete treatment would determine r2r_{2} and rdr_{d} together. Section VI.3 develops the Landau theory of the two-valley regime, r2>r2,cr_{2}>r_{2,c}, as a conditional result.

VI.3 Two-valley Landau theory: exact ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} moduli and selection by loop terms

We now assume that the two-valley regime applies. The two surviving valley fields B1,2B_{1,2} carry the projective representation T1=−i​σ2T_{1}=-i\sigma^{2} (valley swap), T2=−i​σ3T_{2}=-i\sigma^{3}, and a 1/21/\sqrt{2}-mixing rotation with R6=−1R^{6}=-1, and the antiunitary σ​Θ\sigma\Theta closes within the doublet. The invariant theory of this doublet sharpens the moduli-space theorem of Sec. III.3:

  1. (i)

    There is exactly one quartic invariant, (n1+n2)2(n_{1}+n_{2})^{2}, so the entire condensate ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1} is degenerate at quartic order for arbitrary couplings.

  2. (ii)

    At sextic order the invariant space is exactly span⁡{(B†​B)3,x​y​z}\mathrm{span}\{(B^{\dagger}B)^{3},\,xyz\} in Bloch-sphere coordinates, a single tetrahedral anisotropy with extrema ±1/(33)\pm 1/(3\sqrt{3}) on two four-state tetrahedral orbits. The anisotropy is allowed because σ​Θ\sigma\Theta acts as a reflection that preserves x​y​zxyz, whereas in the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-symmetric theory the 90∘90^{\circ} rotations and the inversion remove it.

  3. (iii)

    The on-site quadratic and cubic moments ∑rρr2\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2} and ∑rρr3\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3} are exactly constant on ℂ​ℙ1\mathbb{CP}^{1}, so no on-site term through sextic order can select a state, although the site-density pattern itself varies over the sphere. The three MM-point density amplitudes are the three components of the Bloch vector n^=(x,y,z)\hat{n}=(x,y,z) of the doublet, |ρ⁡(Ma)|=|n^a|​ρ¯/3|\rho(M_{a})|=|\hat{n}_{a}|\bar{\rho}/3, where ρ(𝐤)=N−1∑rρre−i𝐤⋅𝐫\rho(\mathbf{k})=N^{-1}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}\,e^{-i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} and the three MM points are labeled accordingly. The axis points are therefore uni-MM stripes with three density levels {0,1,2}​ρ¯\{0,1,2\}\bar{\rho} on 7272, 288288 and 7272 of the 432432 sites. The tetrahedral points n^=(±1,±1,±1)/3\hat{n}=(\pm 1,\pm 1,\pm 1)/\sqrt{3} are triple-MM crystals with two levels, (1∓1/3)​ρ¯=0.42265​ρ¯(1\mp 1/\sqrt{3})\bar{\rho}=0.42265\,\bar{\rho} and 1.57735​ρ¯1.57735\,\bar{\rho}, each on half the sites (∑rρr4\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{4} varies by 7%7\% between them).

Intersite loop terms resolve the degeneracy. The simplest is the triangle-loop sextic ∑△Re​∏(i​j)∈△B¯i​ti​j​Bj\sum_{\triangle}\mathrm{Re}\prod_{(ij)\in\triangle}\bar{B}_{i}t_{ij}B_{j}. For a condensate, ∏(i​j)∈△B¯i​ti​j​Bj=(∏(i​j)∈△ti​j)​∏i∈△ρi\prod_{(ij)\in\triangle}\bar{B}_{i}t_{ij}B_{j}=\big(\prod_{(ij)\in\triangle}t_{ij}\big)\prod_{i\in\triangle}\rho_{i}, so this term reduces to the flux-weighted three-site density product t13cosθ△∑△ρiρjρk∝(1+xyz)t_{1}^{3}\cos\theta_{\triangle}\sum_{\triangle}\rho_{i}\rho_{j}\rho_{k}\propto(1+xyz). Selection in the doped chiral state is made by intersite density correlations on the triangles, which no on-site moment through cubic order can detect. The two extremal states are triple-MM chiral chargon crystals that are density conjugates of one another (ρ→2​ρ¯−ρ\rho\to 2\bar{\rho}-\rho, which exchanges high- and low-density sites and keeps the same two-level histogram) with distinct loop-current circulation patterns. As for phase II-, the sign of the sextic determines the sign of the triple-MM modulation. The weak-coupling loop-current theory of the kagome metals also arrives at a four-state degenerate manifold at its leading order [138].

The symmetric pair composites Bη​Bη′B_{\eta}B_{\eta^{\prime}} of the two-valley theory exhaust the full MM star, with no uniform (Γ\Gamma) channel at quadratic order. Unlike those of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants, these chargon composites do not produce electron pairing. The chiral ansatz is a pure hopping ansatz with invariant gauge group U(1), so it carries no spinon pairing, while the induced electron pair amplitude is linear in the spinon pairing [the B¯+​B¯+​Δsp\bar{B}_{+}\bar{B}_{+}\Delta^{\rm sp} term of Eq. (4), the B+B_{+}-sector counterpart of Eq. (33)]. Every channel of the electron pair field, uniform and finite-momentum alike, therefore vanishes identically for the doped chiral state at this order, provided that the second gauge sector stays gapped, as in Sec. II.3. The MM-star pair composites then do not describe a pair-density-wave superconductor.

The gap that enforces this is now the sector margin E−−E+E_{-}-E_{+}, which plays the role of Δflat\Delta_{\rm flat}. It is 0.15​t10.15\,t_{1} at r2∗=0.33r_{2}^{*}=0.33 and 0.17​t10.17\,t_{1} at r2=0.35r_{2}=0.35 (Sec. VI.2), closes at r2,cr_{2,c}, and shrinks to 0.01​t10.01\,t_{1} at r2=0.35r_{2}=0.35 under the +20%+20\% variation of φ2\varphi_{2} quoted there. At and near the crossing the two sectors form a near-degenerate pair, and whether both condense is then determined by the inter-sector quartic couplings, which we have not computed. If they do, the χ\chi terms of Eq. (4) yield an electron pair amplitude without any spinon pairing, at the momenta of the mixed composites B¯+​B¯−\bar{B}_{+}\bar{B}_{-}, as in the doublet mechanism of the square and triangular lattices [18, 31]. The conclusions below therefore hold for r2r_{2} well above r2,cr_{2,c}, where the B−B_{-} sector is gapped by the quoted margin.

The particle–hole content of the condensate survives, in the form of the triple-MM chiral chargon crystals of (iii). These form an MM-star charge and loop-current crystal, selected by the triangle density correlations of the loop sextic. At the level of the chargon composites this parallels the triangular chiral case, where the uniform d±i​dd\pm id bilinears likewise vanish for the chiral spin liquid and only half of the K/2K/2 pair-density-wave channels survive [31]. The two lattices differ in the finite-momentum content of the surviving composites, which is the full MM star here and the K/2K/2 star there. Uniform chiral superconductivity, the most commonly assumed outcome of doping a Kalmeyer–Laughlin state, is thus not generated by the chargon condensate within the Higgs framework, on kagome as on the triangular lattice [31].

A route to uniform chiral superconductivity outside the Higgs framework remains a distinct, competing scenario. The chargons may form a bosonic integer quantum Hall state, which is itself a d+i​dd+id superconductor [117, 119], and anyon superconductivity in doped chiral topological states is under active study [75, 112, 26, 103, 76, 15, 31]. Unbiased numerics support that route on another lattice. Density-matrix renormalization and determinantal quantum Monte Carlo on the lightly doped triangular Hofstadter–Hubbard model at a quarter flux quantum per triangle find a chiral superconductor with quantized spin Chern number two when either the integer quantum Hall parent or the chiral spin liquid parent is doped. Its pairing correlations decay more slowly than the period-four charge stripes that accompany them [15], and the companion study of Ref. [76] reaches the same conclusion. The kagome tt–JJ numerics of Sec. VII.3 instead find an insulating holon crystal without superconductivity, but the two settings differ in lattice, in flux and in the chirality of the parent.

Within the Higgs framework, at this order and away from the sector crossing, a doped kagome CSL is therefore predicted to be a nonsuperconducting MM-star charge and current crystal.

The emergent gauge field of the chiral state differs from the Maxwell field of the DSL. Both spin species occupy bands of Chern number one, which is the Kalmeyer–Laughlin class identified in Sec. VI.1, so integrating out the spinons leaves a Chern–Simons term at level two, and a single chargon of unit gauge charge carries statistical angle π/2\pi/2. The Landau theory of Sec. VI.3 describes the mean-field condensation of these semionic chargons, the chiral-metal branch of the analysis of Song, Vishwanath and Zhang [117]. The other branch of that analysis, a bosonic integer quantum Hall state of the chargons that descends to a d+i​dd+id superconductor, is the competing scenario mentioned above. Any Higgs phase built on the chiral state also inherits the spinon Chern number, because the condensate locks the emergent gauge field to the electromagnetic one. The MM-star crystal of the two-valley regime would be a chiral metal with an intrinsic anomalous Hall response in addition to the loop currents of (iii).

The one existing numerical study of a doped kagome chiral spin liquid points the same way. Peng et al. [102] doped the tt–JJ–JχJ_{\chi} model by density-matrix renormalization on six- and eight-leg cylinders at δ=1/24\delta=1/24 to 1/121/12. The model has nearest-neighbor hopping only, with t=3t=3, J=1J=1 and Jχ=0.5J_{\chi}=0.5, deep in the chiral phase. They found a stripe crystal of spinless holons with one hole per emergent cell, no doping-induced magnetic order, and pair correlations decaying exponentially within one unit cell, an insulating charge crystal without superconductivity like the doped tt–JJ liquids of the same work (Sec. VII.3). The result is consistent with the nonsuperconducting outcome derived here. The crystal found there is, however, a stripe and not a triple-MM crystal, and a nearest-neighbor-only model gives the chargon no bare second-neighbor hopping, so the model lies in the four-valley regime below the sector crossing (Sec. VI.2), outside the two-valley theory treated here.

VII The doped case

VII.1 Finite density: the Gross–Pitaevskii regime

Doping the DSL at fixed fractionalization is expected to yield a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL∗) [110, 14, 9]. This expectation is taken over from the square-lattice construction. It presupposes the binding energy of a chargon to a spinon in the presence of the gapless compact U⁡(1)U(1) gauge field of the DSL and the scaling dimensions of the monopoles once Fermi pockets are present, and we establish neither here. In this state the chargons remain gapped, and most of the doped charge is carried by Fermi pockets of chargon–spinon bound states, which are the electron-like quasiparticles. The condensate analysis of the preceding sections does not apply to it.

The Luttinger count depends on neither of these inputs. The pocket volume counts the doped density pp, i.e. 3​p3p holes per three-site cell. A conventional metal at the same filling would instead have a large Fermi surface in the half-filled middle kagome band, with 1+3​p1+3p holes per cell (1/3+p1/3+p per site). The rest of the charge is carried by the fractionalized insulating background.

The Higgs transition out of FL∗ is reached when the chargon gap closes. At nonzero density the Landau theory acquires a first-order time derivative [31], while the potential of Eq. (12) is unchanged. The dynamical exponent is then z=2z=2, so the two-loop check of Appendix D, made for the relativistic theory of the undoped transition, does not carry over. The protection of the Hubbard ray (Sec. III.4) does carry over, because it follows from symmetry alone. The charge carried by the condensate is the Noether density of the physical U⁡(1)U(1). Besides the usual derivative contribution, it contains a term κ​∑ηnη\kappa\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta}, with κ\kappa set by the first-order time derivative, so it is not ∑ηnη\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta} itself. Here κ\kappa is a nonuniversal coefficient determined by the microscopic dynamics and, in general, by the chemical potential. The doping constrains the sum of the pocket and condensate charges, not ∑ηnη\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta}.

The opposite limit, in which all of the doped charge resides in the chargon condensate (the holon picture of Ref. [75]), is described by the lattice Gross–Pitaevskii functional of the chargon hopping problem,

E⁡[B]\displaystyle E[B] =∑⟨i​j⟩t​si​j​(B¯𝒊,+​B𝒋,+−B¯𝒊,−​B𝒋,−)+H.c.\displaystyle=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}t\,s_{ij}\bigl(\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},+}B_{{\bm{j}},+}-\bar{B}_{{\bm{i}},-}B_{{\bm{j}},-}\bigr)+{\rm H.c.}
+U2∑rρr2,ρr=|Br,+|2+|Br,−|2,\displaystyle\quad+\frac{U}{2}\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2}\,,\qquad\rho_{r}=|B_{r,+}|^{2}+|B_{r,-}|^{2}, (36)

where the hopping term is Eq. (3) with tt the chargon hopping. We minimize it on the 12×1212\times 12 torus with the link signs si​js_{ij} of the [0,π][0,\pi] ansatz, keeping both gauge components, at fixed total chargon number ∑rρr=x​N\sum_{r}\rho_{r}=xN.

Fixing the total chargon number does not impose the site-resolved Gauss law, which is then violated at the order of the modulation itself. Imposing it suppresses the density modulation by factors of 1818 and 4444 at x=1/12x=1/12 and 1/61/6, and the physical bond currents by the smaller factors 1.41.4 to 7.07.0 across x=1/36x=1/36 to 1/61/6. The complex valley coefficients, and with them the point on the moduli space, are unchanged to the figures we resolve. At x=1/36x=1/36 and UB/tB=4U_{B}/t_{B}=4 the constrained theory lies inside a miscibility gap, which is absent at UB/tB=16U_{B}/t_{B}=16 and at the physical 6060 to 8080. There its homogeneous state is a long-wavelength inhomogeneity whose root-mean-square contrast is only 1.21.2 times below the unconstrained one (Appendix B).

The symmetry classification of each candidate crystal survives this suppression, because it follows from the projective symmetry group and the point on the moduli space independently of the minimization. The densities reported in this section and the next do not survive it. They are properties of an unconstrained trial background and bound the physical modulation from above, but they do not give its local values.

The functional is first order in time, so the chargon number is its conserved charge and the time-derivative term plays no role in the static minimum. Rescaling B→x​BB\to\sqrt{x}\,B shows that the normalized problem depends on U/tU/t and xx only through U​x/tUx/t. The static potential of the projected Landau theory, Eq. (12), is the restriction of Eq. (36) to the four condensation valleys. The full lattice functional differs from it by the admixture of the non-condensing chargon bands, and eliminating these bands at second order gives the microscopic sextic of Secs. IV.1 and IV.3. That admixture selects the state, because for on-site repulsion alone the projected quartic sits on the I/II- boundary. The sextic is larger in magnitude on the II- level set than on the pair sphere, by the ratio 0.456​N0.456N to 0.088​N0.088N of the resolvent elements, and it selects the unbalanced four-valley K/2K/2 crystal of Eq. (25).

For the charge bookkeeping, the unimodular rotor of Sec. II.1, |B+|2+|B−|2=1|B_{+}|^{2}+|B_{-}|^{2}=1 on every site, is relaxed in the standard way to a soft complex doublet [14, 18, 31], and xx is the doped charge per site carried by that doublet. With only B−B_{-} condensed the fusion rule of Eq. (1) gives c↑=B¯−​f↓†c_{\uparrow}=\bar{B}_{-}\,f^{\dagger}_{\downarrow}, so the electron is the particle-hole conjugate of the spinon. The doped charge resides in the chargon number, ∑rBr†​Br=x​N\sum_{r}B_{r}^{\dagger}B_{r}=xN, and the Gauss law (nf−1)+n+−n−=0(n_{f}-1)+n_{+}-n_{-}=0 of Sec. II.1 then fixes the spinon filling at nf=1+xn_{f}=1+x, or 1−x1-x for the conjugate, electron-doped quanta. The electron-like quasiparticles carry the doped density 1∓x1\mp x. When the condensate is projected onto the four low-energy valleys this reads ∑ηnη=x​N\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta}=xN, with the valley Bloch states normalized to unity (Sec. II.1). In the full lattice minimization the interaction-induced higher-band admixture means that the four-valley weight ∑ηnη/(x​N)\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta}/(xN) need not remain equal to unity.

We have minimized this functional for the full chargon doublet, as a mean-field model of the fully condensed regime, at x=1/12x=1/12 and at x=1/3x=1/3 (the “Dirac metal” filling targeted by Ga substitution [90, 104] and by Li intercalation [71] of herbertsmithite), with on-site repulsion U/t=0.5U/t=0.5–1616.

(i) Across both fillings and the full interaction range, direct minimization of the complete chargon doublet converges to a purely B−B_{-} condensate. The same holds once the site-resolved Gauss law is imposed. Then ⟨B+⟩=0\langle B_{+}\rangle=0 is a minimum of the constrained functional, by a margin that stays positive at every doping and coupling tested (Appendix B), in the functional that keeps the number-conserving part of the fusion rule alone. For U​x≤1/3Ux\leq 1/3 the minimizer is the sextic-selected K/2K/2 crystal on the phase-II- manifold. Its valley projection gives (𝒫,𝒳)=(12,−14)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{X})=(\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{4}) to 10−410^{-4}, while the four-valley weight decreases from 0.9990.999 to 0.9810.981 as the interaction-induced higher-band admixture grows.

For U​x≥2/3Ux\geq 2/3, continuation from strong coupling finds pure-B−B_{-} states below the K/2K/2 crystal. They lie lower marginally at U​x=2/3Ux=2/3 (8×10−5​t8\times 10^{-5}\,t per chargon) and by 2.4×10−32.4\times 10^{-3} to 6.9×10−3​t6.9\times 10^{-3}\,t per chargon for U​x≥4/3Ux\geq 4/3. These states still lie on the II- quadric [(𝒫,𝒳)=(0.5000,−0.2500)(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{X})=(0.5000,-0.2500) at U​x=2/3Ux=2/3 and (0.5001,−0.2494)(0.5001,-0.2494) above], but their valley content is unbalanced, their four-valley weight is 0.750.75 to 0.780.78 (0.890.89 at U​x=2/3Ux=2/3), and their density has no residual translation symmetry on the 432432-site torus. The landscape is glassy, and global optimality is not established at any coupling.

The minimizer landing on the II- manifold is consistent with the quartic analysis of Sec. IV.1 and corroborates Sec. IV.3. Because the functional contains on-site repulsion only, its projected quartic lies exactly on the I/II- boundary θU=arctan⁡5\theta_{U}=\arctan\sqrt{5} of the pure projected on-site representative, and the selection is made beyond quartic order. Eliminating the non-condensing chargon bands at second order generates a sextic whose strength on a given condensate is the quadratic form v†​G​vv^{\dagger}Gv. Here vr=ρr​ψrv_{r}=\rho_{r}\psi_{r} is the density-weighted condensate profile and GG the resolvent of the eliminated bands, and a larger value means a lower energy. On the 432432-site torus the form equals 4​(12−6)=38.204(12-\sqrt{6})=38.20 on all of phase I (the value scales with NN). It is constant over the pair sphere, as the moduli theorem of Sec. III.3 requires of any sextic, and it reaches ≃197\simeq 197 (≃0.456​N\simeq 0.456N) at the selected K/2K/2 crystal on the II- quadric.

The selection therefore depends on the interaction, and neither state is singled out as the physical one. For the pure projected on-site representative, the K/2K/2 crystal is selected beyond quartic order. Once the intersite repulsion exceeds the mean-field crossover Vc≃9.3​U2​x/tV_{c}\simeq 9.3\,U^{2}x/t of Eq. (22) (in the U​∑rρr2U\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2} normalization of Sec. IV.1, or 2.3​U2​x/t2.3\,U^{2}x/t in the (U/2)​∑rρr2(U/2)\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2} normalization of this section), i.e. for V/UV/U of order U​x/tUx/t, the phase-I MM state is selected instead.

The resulting state is a K/2K/2-modulated chargon Higgs phase rather than a superfluid. With only B−B_{-} condensed, the diagonal combination QEM−QgQ_{\rm EM}-Q_{g} of the physical electromagnetic charge QEMQ_{\rm EM} and the emergent gauge charge QgQ_{g} remains unbroken. The condensate therefore carries charge density and loop current but no physical pair amplitude, which would require spinon pairing (Sec. V). Section VII.2 examines the spectrum of its electron-like quasiparticles.

For U​x≤1/3Ux\leq 1/3 its density shares the thirty-six-site cell of the sextic-selected crystal of Sec. IV.3. The functional predicts that the modulation is progressively screened as the coupling grows. The density range is ρ/ρ¯∈(0.47,1.88)\rho/\bar{\rho}\in(0.47,1.88) at U​x=1/24Ux=1/24 (the controlled point U=0.5​tU=0.5t, x=1/12x=1/12) and (0.57,1.65)(0.57,1.65) at U​x≈0.17Ux\approx 0.17, and it narrows to (0.80,1.19)(0.80,1.19) at U​x=4/3Ux=4/3 and to (0.93,1.06)(0.93,1.06) at U​x=16/3Ux=16/3 for the lowest states found there. Those stronger-coupling states break the K/2K/2 superlattice (39%39\% of their modulation power lies off it at U​x=16/3Ux=16/3), but the screening persists. Beyond the weak-coupling points the screening is a prediction of the mean-field functional and is not controlled (see (ii) below).

In its valley content, the minimizer at U​x≈0.17Ux\approx 0.17 is the sextic-selected crystal of Sec. IV.3 itself, and not just another state on the same level set. Its valley projection has ⟨ρ3⟩/ρ¯ 3=2.1443\langle\rho^{3}\rangle/\bar{\rho}^{\,3}=2.1443, which is the closed-form value 2+1/(4​3)2+1/(4\sqrt{3}) of the state selected by the negative-definite on-site sextic. That state is the density conjugate ρ→2​ρ¯−ρ\rho\to 2\bar{\rho}-\rho of the ∑rρr3\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{3} minimizer on the II- level set, for which the value is 2−1/(4​3)2-1/(4\sqrt{3}). The agreement between the lattice functional and the sextic selection holds over the weak-coupling part of the scan, U​x/t≤1/3Ux/t\leq 1/3. At stronger coupling the landscape of Eq. (36) is glassy (Sec. VII.3).

(ii) The flat band is never populated in the scanned regime, in the functional without the pairing block. At mean field the sign of the coupling favors this result, which symmetry does not enforce.
