Because B+B_{+} and B−B_{-} carry equal electric and opposite gauge charge, every gauge- and charge-allowed local coupling between them is a polynomial in the densities ρ±=B±†​B±\rho_{\pm}=B_{\pm}^{\dagger}B_{\pm}. The leading one is the cross term of the on-site repulsion, and it enters with a positive sign. In the normalization used here the functional is (U/2)​∑rρr2(U/2)\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2}, so U​ρU\rho is the Hartree potential and the cross term is U​ρ+​ρ−U\rho_{+}\rho_{-}. In the normalization U​∑rρr2U\sum_{r}\rho_{r}^{2} of Sec. IV.1 the cross term reads 2​U​ρ+​ρ−2U\rho_{+}\rho_{-}, and U​x=16/3Ux=16/3 here corresponds to U​x=8/3Ux=8/3 there. A B−B_{-} condensate of density ρ¯\bar{\rho} therefore raises the B+B_{+} mass by U​ρ¯U\bar{\rho}.

The stability gap nevertheless narrows with coupling. The same diagonal Hartree potential U​ρU\rho acts in both gauge sectors and raises the B+B_{+} bottom, for the K/2K/2 crystal by 0.96​U​ρ¯0.96\,U\bar{\rho} at U​x=16/3Ux=16/3. The condensate chemical potential, however, rises by at least U⁡⟨ρ2⟩/ρ¯≥U​ρ¯U\langle\rho^{2}\rangle/\bar{\rho}\geq U\bar{\rho} for a modulated density, and by 1.01​U​ρ¯1.01\,U\bar{\rho} for the K/2K/2 crystal at U​x=16/3Ux=16/3 once the condensate’s own kinetic-energy cost is included. The stability gap against infinitesimal B+B_{+} admixture, λmin​(H++U​ρ)−μ−\lambda_{\min}(H_{+}+U\rho)-\mu_{-}, decreases from the bare (6−1)​t≃1.449​t(\sqrt{6}-1)t\simeq 1.449\,t to about 1.14​t1.14\,t at U​x=16/3Ux=16/3, the largest coupling of the scan. A separate continuation of the lowest state to U​x=40Ux=40 gives 1.09​t1.09\,t. For the K/2K/2 crystal itself, which is a higher-lying local minimum for U​x≥2/3Ux\geq 2/3, the corresponding values are 1.154​t1.154\,t and 1.10​t1.10\,t. For a uniform condensate density the two sectors shift rigidly by the same Hartree energy, and the gap stays at (6−1)​t(\sqrt{6}-1)t exactly. The whole decrease is therefore an effect of the density modulation.

These values refer to the lowest states found: the K/2K/2 crystal of the II- manifold for U​x≤1/3Ux\leq 1/3 and the states described under (i) above it. The gap depends on the state. A condensate constrained to the single-valley Bloch sector of the phase-I stripe is a stationary point of the functional but not its minimizer. Its self-consistent gap is 1.29​t1.29\,t at U​x=1/6Ux=1/6 and 0.30​t0.30\,t at U​x=16/3Ux=16/3. The gap is smaller here because the flat multiplet can occupy the stripe’s low-density sublattice, but it stays positive. This stripe value, computed with on-site repulsion alone, illustrates the state dependence and is not a prediction for the gap of the intersite-selected phase-I regime. The gap remains positive throughout, and neither full-doublet minimization nor fixed-B+B_{+}-weight scans find a competing mixed-sector state. All of these are Hartree–Gross–Pitaevskii statements about a flat multiplet that is 144-fold degenerate on the 432-site torus, and they indicate stability at mean field, within the local potential.

Beyond the local potential, B+B_{+} couples to the spinon sector through the gauge-neutral hopping term linear in B+B_{+} displayed in Sec. II.3 [Fig. 8(a)]. In the U(1) state this term gives B+B_{+} a second-order self-energy whose intermediate states contain two spinons. The number is fixed by the Gauss law of Sec. II.1, since converting a B+B_{+} quantum into a B−B_{-} raises nfn_{f} by two. These intermediate states span [0.43,2.56]​tsp[0.43,2.56]\,t_{\rm sp}, a spinon scale, whereas Δflat=(6−1)​tB\Delta_{\rm flat}=(\sqrt{6}-1)t_{B} is set by the chargon scale, and the two are far apart. With tsp≃c1​Jt_{\rm sp}\simeq c_{1}J and tB=2​c1​|tc|t_{B}=2c_{1}|t_{c}| (Sec. II.2), their ratio is tsp/tB=2​|tc|/U=0.056t_{\rm sp}/t_{B}=2|t_{c}|/U=0.056 to 0.0720.072 over the parameter range of Sec. VIII. Here the exchange is held at its measured value, so tct_{c} and UU are not independent. The continuum reaches Δflat\Delta_{\rm flat} only for tsp/tB>0.566t_{\rm sp}/t_{B}>0.566, eight to ten times the physical ratio, so against the bare splitting the decay channel B+→B−+B_{+}\to B_{-}+ two spinons is closed. This comparison sets a dressed continuum against an undressed level, and a fully dressed evaluation lies beyond the present treatment.

The on-shell spectral shift and the static stability correction are distinct, nonadditive quantities. The spectral position of the branch is set by the retarded self-energy on shell, at ω=Δflat\omega=\Delta_{\rm flat}, which lies above every intermediate state. There the shift is repulsive, +(1.5CLOSE+(1.5 to OPEN2.0)​x​tc2/tB2.0)\,x\,t_{c}^{2}/t_{B} across the 144144 states. It moves the lowest level up from Δflat=1.449​tB\Delta_{\rm flat}=1.449\,t_{B} to 1.681.68 and 2.13​tB2.13\,t_{B} at x=1/36x=1/36 and x=1/12x=1/12 for the stripe, and to 1.691.69 and 2.17​tB2.17\,t_{B} for the K/2K/2 crystal. Whether the sector condenses, which is what the width of the window measures, is governed by the static limit ω→0\omega\to 0, where every denominator reverses sign and the shift is attractive, −(0.4CLOSE-(0.4 to OPEN1.2)​x​tc2/tsp1.2)\,x\,t_{c}^{2}/t_{\rm sp}. The upward shift of the high-energy branch thus carries no gain in stability.

At the physical scales the static shift is not controlled. With tc2/(tsp​tB)=2.56​ut_{c}^{2}/(t_{\rm sp}t_{B})=2.56\,u and u=U/|tc|=28u=U/|t_{c}|=28 to 3636 (Sec. VIII), it already amounts to 0.60.6 to 2.12.1 times Δflat\Delta_{\rm flat} at x=1/36x=1/36, and to 1.61.6 to 6.36.3 times at x=1/12x=1/12. This tracks the expansion parameter tc​x/tspt_{c}x/t_{\rm sp} of Sec. VII.2, which is of order one at the lowest commensuration and larger above it. The separation of scales closes the decay channel against the bare splitting, but neither shift fixes the width of the window at physical coupling.

The emergent gauge field also couples the flat sector to the condensate directly [Fig. 8(b)]. Because B+B_{+} and B−B_{-} carry opposite emergent gauge charge, it mediates an attraction between a B+B_{+} quantum and the B−B_{-} condensate, screened only beyond a length set by the doping. The B+B_{+} states are exactly flat, so an arbitrarily weak attraction binds. A bound B+B_{+} quantum is gauge neutral with physical charge 2​e2e (Sec. II.3), and its condensation would restore superconductivity at the U⁡(1)U(1) level. A bound state with binding energy EBE_{B} lies at Δflat−EB\Delta_{\rm flat}-E_{B}, however, which is still above the condensate unless EBE_{B} exceeds Δflat\Delta_{\rm flat}. Moreover, once the condensate response and the polarization of the Dirac spinons are included, the kernel in the condensed gauge theory is not a two-body potential. The positive cross-quartic U​ρ+​ρ−U\rho_{+}\rho_{-} and the Gross–Pitaevskii stability gap run against binding. The static spinon-continuum shift runs toward it, by an amount the second-order treatment does not control. A further channel exists at the same order. The fusion rule that gives B+B_{+} its hopping, applied to the electron hopping, also pairs the spinons through a singlet field proportional to B+​B¯−B_{+}\bar{B}_{-}, so the spinon sector acquires a pairing block that enters the energy at the same order in B+B_{+} as the Hartree gap and is absent from it. Its effect requires an all-orders treatment of the spinon sector at each chargon configuration, which lies beyond this paper. The conclusion that the condensed phase does not superconduct is therefore a mean-field statement, valid at the Hartree level for B+B_{+}. This dynamical question separates the condensation route from the variational superconducting scenario of Sec. VII.3.

The functional also has a limited domain of validity. Over the scanned range U​x/W−Ux/W_{-} runs from 0.060.06 to 7.47.4, where W−=(6−3)​tW_{-}=(\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{3})\,t is the width of the lowest B−B_{-} band (Sec. II.3). Only the U/t=0.5U/t=0.5 points are therefore controlled. The others are properties of the mean-field functional and say nothing about the strong-coupling problem. Flat-band-assisted chargon crystallization as a strong-coupling effect beyond Gross–Pitaevskii thus remains a conjecture, suggested but not established by these results.

(iii) The natural commensurate fillings of the charge-crystal channels are set by one chargon per crystal cell: x=1/6x=1/6 for the uni-MM stripe (six-site cell), x=1/12x=1/12 for the 2×22\times 2 crystal (twelve sites), and x=1/36x=1/36 for the thirty-six-site 12×12\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12} K/2K/2 crystal realized both by the sextic selection and by the GP minimizer.

These are commensurate fillings of the composite stars, but the functional does not lock in to them. The crystal cell is fixed by the valley momenta at every xx and the Gross–Pitaevskii energy is analytic in xx, so nothing in the functional singles out one chargon per cell. A true lock-in, with a cusp in the energy or an insulating plateau, would require the hard-core physics of chargons in their own superlattice, which lies beyond the functional [see (ii)]. Throughout, “commensurate filling” is meant in this sense.

The KK-star composite is not a charge channel in this construction. Its site-density form factor and its gauge-invariant bond charge out to third-neighbor range vanish identically at KK for every condensate, although it can carry loop current (Sec. IV.4). The 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} cell therefore defines no charge-crystal endpoint at x=1/9x=1/9. Special two-valley representatives of the K/2K/2 family have smaller eighteen-site cells (x=1/18x=1/18), so the K/2K/2 commensuration depends on the representative. For U​x≥2/3Ux\geq 2/3 a broadened search (continuation from strong coupling and many starts) does find pure-B−B_{-} states below the K/2K/2 crystal, described under (i). No mixed-sector state appeared in the fixed-B+B_{+}-weight scans or in unrestricted minimization over the full doublet started from any of them.

At the Gross–Pitaevskii level the theory thus predicts a K/2K/2-modulated chargon Higgs phase, which can become superconducting only through the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} channel λ\lambda of Sec. V. We examine its electron-like quasiparticles next. The crystallization seen in strong-coupling numerics must come from physics beyond the functional (Sec. VII.3).

VII.2 Electron spectrum in the condensed phase

The condensates of Sec. VII.1 fix the charge and current pattern of the Higgs phase. Whether it conducts is set by the spinon spectrum in their presence. The spectra of this section are computed on those condensates and inherit their status. The background satisfies the Gauss law on average but not site by site, and a constraint-consistent saddle suppresses its density modulation by up to a factor of 4444 and its currents by up to a factor of 77 (Appendix B).

With only B−B_{-} condensed, Eq. (1) gives c↑=B¯−​f↓†c_{\uparrow}=\bar{B}_{-}f^{\dagger}_{\downarrow} (Sec. VII.1), so the physical electron hopping −tc∑⟨i​j⟩(ci†cj+H.c.)-t_{c}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(c^{\dagger}_{i}c_{j}+\mathrm{H.c.}) acts on the spinons, at mean field, as the additional hopping tc​B¯i​Bjt_{c}\bar{B}_{i}B_{j}. The spinon link field becomes −t​si​j​[1−(tc/t)​B¯i​si​j​Bj]-t\,s_{ij}\,[1-(t_{c}/t)\,\bar{B}_{i}s_{ij}B_{j}], which is the ansatz multiplied by the gauge-invariant bond amplitude of the condensate. Here tt is the spinon hopping, an exchange-scale quantity (Sec. II.2). The expansion parameter of the linear-order statements below is therefore tc​x/tt_{c}x/t, not xx. With t≃c1​Jt\simeq c_{1}J and the parameters of Sec. VIII it is of order one already at x=1/36x=1/36, and we present the calculation, in units of the spinon hopping, as the leading term of that expansion.

The node shifts and the inter-node coupling below are matrix elements of tc​B¯i​Bjt_{c}\bar{B}_{i}B_{j} between nodal states and scale with tct_{c}. The second-order gaps scale as tc2/tt_{c}^{2}/t, and these are the quantities that the small-ratio assumption affects. We have also diagonalized the same 432×432432\times 432 problem non-perturbatively, with the spinon hopping set to c1​Jc_{1}J and the feedback at full strength, for which tc​x/t=0.7t_{c}x/t=0.7 to 8.78.7 over the doping window and the parameter range of Sec. VIII. This leaves the Gauss-law pocket structure intact, with Luttinger volume xx and a single carrier sign at every coupling, and it does not change the ordering of the three condensates by spinon energy. It does change the near-degeneracy at nf=1n_{f}=1. There the dressed bands acquire an overlap of 0.040.04 to 0.44​c1​J0.44\,c_{1}J on the stripe, so the small nf=1n_{f}=1 gaps quoted below describe only the weak-feedback limit. The decoupling of Sec. II.1 fixes the sign of tct_{c} relative to tt. With B−B_{-} the condensed component, tc<0t_{c}<0 (the opposite combination, tc>0t_{c}>0 with B+B_{+} condensed, gives the complex-conjugate induced hopping and an identical spectrum).

We have diagonalized this Hamiltonian on the 12×1212\times 12 torus for the uni-MM stripe and the triple-MM state of Sec. IV.2 and for the K/2K/2 crystal selected by the on-site sextic in Sec. IV.3, which is the state to which the minimizer of Sec. VII.1 converges at weak coupling. We take ∑r|Br|2=x​N\sum_{r}|B_{r}|^{2}=xN and tc=−tt_{c}=-t, with the sign fixed in Sec. II.1, for 0.005≤x≤0.170.005\leq x\leq 0.17, and minimize the direct gap at the node energy over twisted boundary conditions. The spinon filling is nf=1+xn_{f}=1+x for hole doping and 1−x1-x for electron doping (Sec. II.1). The two cases are not mirror images, because the spinon bands are not particle–hole symmetric. On the 12×1212\times 12 torus N⁡(1±x)/2N(1\pm x)/2 is an integer at the three commensurate dopings x=1/6x=1/6, 1/121/12 and 1/361/36, and (iv) below places the Fermi level at these dopings.

(i) At linear order in xx none of the three condensates opens a per-node Dirac mass. The valley densities enter the spinon problem only through the conserved MM-point currents of Sec. IV.4, which shift the two nodes in energy and momentum without generating a mass term, and a site-diagonal potential proportional to the condensate density does not generate one either. The only linear-order gap is the inter-node one of the triple-MM state below, and a 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} projection of the induced perturbation onto the four nodal states reproduces the lattice slopes in the limit x→0x\to 0.

(ii) The uni-MM stripe leaves both nodes gapless at every xx studied (direct gap at the node energy below 10−6​t10^{-6}\,t), and its stabilizer, of order 24, forbids a per-node Dirac mass and any inter-node coupling at all orders. The linear term moves the nodes to εF+1.18​x​t\varepsilon_{F}+1.18\,xt and εF+0.09​x​t\varepsilon_{F}+0.09\,xt, with εF=(3−1)​t\varepsilon_{F}=(\sqrt{3}-1)t the node energy of the half-filled parent.

(iii) The triple-MM state couples the two nodes, |V12|=0.63​x​t|V_{12}|=0.63\,xt, and opens an inter-node gap at the node energy, Δ≃0.046​x​t−0.12​x2​t\Delta\simeq 0.046\,xt-0.12\,x^{2}t over the scanned range (the 𝐤⋅𝐩\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p} slope is 0.049​t0.049\,t), i.e. 3×10−3​t3\times 10^{-3}\,t at its commensurate filling x=1/12x=1/12. The K/2K/2 crystal, for which a per-node mass is symmetry-allowed but absent from the induced perturbation at linear order, opens a gap at the node energy only at second order, Δ≃0.13\Delta\simeq 0.13 to 0.14​x2​t0.14\,x^{2}t for x≤0.04x\leq 0.04 (falling to 0.11​x2​t0.11\,x^{2}t at x=0.1x=0.1), i.e. 1.0×10−4​t1.0\times 10^{-4}\,t at its commensurate filling x=1/36x=1/36 and 1.1×10−3​t1.1\times 10^{-3}\,t at x=0.1x=0.1.

(iv) Because the Gauss law places the spinons at nf=1±xn_{f}=1\pm x, away from half filling, conduction is governed by the spectrum at the Fermi level and not at the nodes. At nf=1+xn_{f}=1+x (hole doping) the Fermi level lies 0.340.34 to 0.77​t0.77\,t above both shifted nodes for the stripe, the triple-MM state and the K/2K/2 crystal at their commensurate dopings. At nf=1−xn_{f}=1-x (electron doping) it lies 0.430.43 to 1.35​t1.35\,t below them. In every case there is no gap at the Fermi level.

All three condensates are metals at mean field (Fig. 9). Their electron-like quasiparticles form Fermi surfaces of one carrier sign around the two nodes, with total Luttinger volume xx. These are closed pockets, with one exception. For the stripe at x=1/6x=1/6 the Fermi level sits 0.01​t0.01\,t above the saddle point of the pocket band around the lower node, and that sheet is open along 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1}. The condensate-induced gaps of (iii) lie 0.340.34 to 0.83​t0.83\,t from the Fermi level and do not affect conduction. Counting gives the same answer without diagonalization. With the feedback included, the spinon Bloch cell coincides with the condensate cell of six, twelve or thirty-six sites. This cell holds 3.53.5, 6.56.5 or 18.518.5 spinons per spin at nf=1+xn_{f}=1+x (2.52.5, 5.55.5 or 17.517.5 at 1−x1-x). Because these numbers are half-integers, no spin-degenerate band insulator exists at any of the three lock-ins.

An insulating gap at the commensurate fillings must come from physics beyond mean field, such as confinement, loss of single-chargon coherence, further-neighbor feedback of the condensate on the spinon hopping, or interactions beyond the quadratic spinon problem. We compute none of these, so we do not claim an insulating gap of order tt on the basis of this calculation. Counting constrains such physics. At x=1/nsx=1/n_{s} the nsn_{s}-site cell holds ns∓1n_{s}\mp 1 electrons for hole or electron doping, an odd number for each of the three crystals (ns=6n_{s}=6, 1212, 3636). By the Lieb–Schultz–Mattis theorem in its higher-dimensional form [82, 99, 42] no symmetric gapped insulator exists at these fillings. An insulator there must either break a further symmetry, for instance by doubling the period or ordering magnetically, or carry topological order. Spinon pairing cannot produce topological order while the chargon stays condensed. Since B−B_{-} carries unit gauge charge, the Higgs phase retains no gauge structure for a charge-two spinon pair to restore, and by Eq. (4) paired spinons in the presence of the condensate give a physical charge-2​e2e superconductor rather than a charge-conserving insulator. A gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} liquid of the remaining spins requires the chargons first to lose single-particle coherence, after which paired spinons can provide it. The same constraint applies to the insulating holon crystals of the strong-coupling numerics (Sec. VII.3).

Together with Sec. VII.1, these results characterize the condensed phase as a chargon Higgs phase with the diagonal U(1) QEM−QgQ_{\rm EM}-Q_{g} unbroken and no superfluid response. It carries the charge density and loop currents of Sec. IV.4, and at mean field its electron-like quasiparticles are metallic, with pockets of volume xx. The electron spectral function is the condensate-weighted particle–hole conjugate of the spinon spectrum, and the doped charge resides in the condensate, as the bookkeeping of Sec. VII.1 prescribes.

Because the condensing field carries unit gauge charge, the Higgs phase has no residual gauge structure and is continuously connected to a conventional charge-ordered metal [33]. Luttinger’s theorem therefore applies to its electron-like quasiparticles in the enlarged cell. The ns​(1∓x)n_{s}(1\mp x) electrons per nsn_{s}-site cell fill half of the reduced zone per spin, which is the count of the parent’s Dirac nodes, plus or minus a signed pocket volume xx (Sec. VII.4). The theorem fixes this signed volume only modulo filled bands. That the pockets have one carrier sign, with no compensating pocket elsewhere and no intervening Lifshitz transition, is a property of the band parameters we have scanned, and we claim it only for those crystals and values of xx.

VII.3 Strong coupling: holon crystals and the two routes

This subsection compares the symmetry and commensuration content of the condensate theory with published strong-coupling numerics and contains no energetics of its own. Ko, Lee, and Wen [75] already posed the question of the strong-coupling fate of the doped kagome spin liquid. Their holon band coincides with our dispersive sector (B−B_{-} in the labeling of Eq. (1), B+B_{+} in their t>0t>0 convention, Sec. II.3), and the translation sector of its projective representation is their Eq. (30) (Sec. III.1). From the same four minima they distinguished two states.

For the flux-free state, their Fermi-pocket state, they observe that “by Bose statistics the holons will condense at each quadratic band bottom” [75]. The Landau theory of Secs. III.2 and IV tests this statement and finds that a balanced occupation of the four band bottoms is selected in neither limit. On-site repulsion selects nothing among the valley occupations at θU\theta_{U}, nearest-neighbor repulsion tilts the quartic minimum to the pair condensate of phase I, and the microscopically generated sextic tilts it to the unbalanced four-valley K/2K/2 crystal of phase II- (Sec. IV.1).

Their second state, which they argued is favored at low doping (spinon gain ∝\propto flux3/2 versus holon cost ∝\propto flux2), arises from a different mechanism. An emergent uniform flux rearranges holons and spinons into Landau levels, the holons form four ν=1/2\nu=1/2 Laughlin states, and the outcome is a time-reversal-breaking anyon superconductor with h​c/4​ehc/4e vortices. That construction rests on their Landau-level energetics and assumes no symmetric condensate, and we do not contest it on its own terms. The present work instead develops the condensation route systematically, with the Landau theory in place of a symmetric valley occupation.

Strong-coupling numerics can discriminate between the two routes. Density-matrix renormalization on the lightly doped kagome tt–JJ model finds an insulating crystal of spinless, unpaired holons, the chargon degree of freedom of the present theory, with no superconductivity (ξSC≲1.3\xi_{\rm SC}\lesssim 1.3 lattice spacings for all δ≤11%\delta\leq 11\%) [62, 102]. On the square lattice, by contrast, the corresponding crystal consists of singlet hole (holon) pairs [27, 62], objects that in the gauge-doublet language require both gauge components (Sec. II.3). The strongly renormalized, valence-bond-dressed holon reported there also identifies the strong-coupling ingredients (mass enhancement, induced repulsion) that undercut the Landau-level energetics of Ref. [75] and are absent from the Gross–Pitaevskii functional.

Whether these studies find a stripe or a crystal depends on geometry and doping, through a competition among cells set by 1/δ1/\delta that lies outside the MM-star sector to which our moduli theorem applies. The tensor-network phase diagram of Ref. [133] connects to our commensurate endpoint. At δ=1/6\delta=1/6 the C3C_{3}-symmetric trihexagonal 2×22\times 2 crystal (two holes per cell) and a four-hole Wigner crystal in a 2×42\times 4 cell are nearly degenerate, and the 2×12\times 1 stripe is close in energy. This near degeneracy of C3C_{3}-symmetric and unidirectional charge crystals parallels the uni-MM/tri-MM competition of Sec. IV.2, but it is not the same competition.

The doped phase diagram of Ref. [133] parallels the structure found here across its full range:

  1. (i)

    insulating charge crystals for δ<0.27\delta<0.27;

  2. (ii)

    a non-Fermi-liquid window 0.27<δ<0.320.27<\delta<0.32 in which the extended-ss (our β\beta-channel) order dies in the extrapolation;

  3. (iii)

    for 0.32<δ<1/30.32<\delta<1/3, a translation-invariant paired state that the authors call a “pair-density wave” because the nearest-neighbor pair amplitude alternates in sign between the up- and down-triangles of their 1×11\times 1 cell, Δ=(Δa,Δb,Δa,Δb,Δa,Δb)\Delta=(\Delta_{a},\Delta_{b},\Delta_{a},\Delta_{b},\Delta_{a},\Delta_{b}) with Δa>0>Δb\Delta_{a}>0>\Delta_{b} on the six bonds.

The last is the Q=0Q=0, up/down-triangle sign-alternating structure of our α\alpha channel [133], and d+i​dd+id is never the ground state, as Sec. V.3 requires. Their pairing ansatz is uniform over a 1×11\times 1 cell and cannot host the MM-star or K/2K/2-star modulations. That work therefore neither tests nor contradicts the finite-momentum pair content predicted here.

Adding next-nearest-neighbor couplings melts the holon crystal into a Fermi-liquid-like state [61], which provides a microscopic control parameter for the crystal-to-condensate transition. The same study finds a distinct commensurate crystal reappearing at δ=1/9\delta=1/9 [61], the filling of one chargon per 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} cell. Its pattern has not been identified, and it has no counterpart among the charge composites of Table 2. In this construction the KK-star composite carries no site charge and no bond charge out to third-neighbor range, though it can carry loop current (Sec. IV.4). A 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} charge crystal at δ=1/9\delta=1/9 falls outside the charge content of the leading condensate composites.

The most recent density-matrix renormalization results sharpen this correspondence [60]. In the nearest-neighbor tt–JJ model, doping alone melts the holon Wigner crystal at δ≈0.15\delta\approx 0.15, just below the densest commensurate endpoint x=1/6x=1/6 of the crystal ladder. The result is a uniform metallic phase with power-law correlations and no hole pairing out to δ=0.36\delta=0.36. The absence of superconductivity in the doped DSL therefore persists on both sides of the melting transition.

In the crystal regime each emergent cell holds one hole, and stripe patterns are reported at δ=1/36\delta=1/36–1/181/18 [62, 60]. These fillings coincide with the K/2K/2-crystal commensurations of Sec. VII.1. The coincidence is suggestive, but we do not identify the two. The reported stripes are unidirectional orders with emergent cells of 36 to 18 sites, whose period depends on the cylinder geometry as well as on the filling. They are neither the six-site MM stripe of Sec. IV.2 nor the thirty-six-site, five-level K/2K/2 crystal.

Reference [60] leaves open whether the melted phase is a conventional or a fractionalized Fermi liquid. In the chargon theory the natural candidate is the FL* of uncondensed chargons, and the Hall number of Sec. VII.4 distinguishes the two. In a narrow window at δ=1/3\delta=1/3 the same calculations find a pseudogap-like precursor state with a single-particle gap and strongly enhanced pairing, adjacent to the tensor-network α\alpha-channel pairing window above. It disappears on the wider Ly=4L_{y}=4 cylinder in the same work, and its fate in two dimensions remains open [60].

Variational studies point the same way. The earliest Monte Carlo study of the doped kagome DSL found the flux collapsing under doping toward a zero-flux state with valence-bond order [37]. Its refined Star-of-David pattern is optimal at δ=1/12\delta=1/12, with one hole per twelve-site cell and repulsive interactions [38]. Its cell is the 2×22\times 2 commensuration of Sec. VII.1, identified variationally a decade before the present framework.

Every result from Sec. II.3 onward assumes the link field of the undoped ansatz (Sec. II.1), and the chargon theory can estimate where that collapse sets in. A doped carrier at the chargon band bottom gains (3−6)​t≃0.55​t(3-\sqrt{6})\,t\simeq 0.55\,t if the flux pattern collapses to a flux-free one (band bottom −4​t-4t against −(1+6)​t-(1+\sqrt{6})\,t), with tt the chargon hopping of Sec. II.3. The half-filled spinon sector, in contrast, prefers the parent pattern by 0.04230.0423 times the spinon hopping per site. The two saddle points therefore cross at x∗=Δ​Esp​tsp/[(3−6)​tB]≃0.003x^{*}=\Delta E_{\rm sp}\,t_{\rm sp}/[(3-\sqrt{6})\,t_{B}]\simeq 0.003 to 0.0070.007 over the parameter range of Sec. VIII, and at 0.0770.077 if the spinon hopping is set equal to the chargon hopping. Below x∗x^{*} the parent link field is stable against flux collapse, the only competitor tested here. Above it the flux-collapsed states are the competitors, and the gauge-rotated states of Ref. [64] overtake them only at the smallest dopings for the largest t/Jt/J studied there. The estimate is crude. It places every carrier at the band bottom and neglects the doping dependence of the spinon energy. Its message nevertheless agrees with the variational results: the rigid-background assumption restricts the theory to the dilute end of the doping window of Sec. VIII. The commensurate fillings of that section sit at or above this range. The lowest, x=1/36=0.028x=1/36=0.028, falls below x∗x^{*} only for tsp=tBt_{\rm sp}=t_{B}, which gives x∗=0.077x^{*}=0.077, and x=1/12x=1/12 and 1/61/6 lie above it for every choice. The crystals at those fillings are predicted on the assumption that the parent flux survives the doping, which the estimate does not establish.

A later study enlarged the variational space by site-dependent SU(2) gauge rotations of the doped ansatz [64]. These degrees of freedom amount to a static chargon configuration. The study found that this class overtakes the flux-collapsed states at low doping and selects a 2×22\times 2, time-reversal- and inversion-breaking nematic pair-density wave with a Bogoliubov Fermi surface and a coexisting 2×22\times 2 charge modulation. This combination of cell, nematicity and broken time-reversal and inversion symmetry matches the MM-star chargon condensates of Sec. IV, here realized in projected wave functions. That superconducting scenario and the charge-order-first route developed here differ in the fate of the flat sector. A physical pair amplitude without spinon pairing requires both gauge components, whereas the Gross–Pitaevskii minimization above finds ⟨B+⟩=0\langle B_{+}\rangle=0 protected, and the density-matrix renormalization results, which find no hole pairing, are consistent with it. Whether the flat sector condenses is a dynamical question that symmetry leaves open.

Experimentally, the realized electron-doped series, Li-intercalated herbertsmithite [71], remains insulating at every composition studied, through the nominal Dirac-metal point. The Ga-substituted series is insulating for a different reason. Its Ga3+ charge is compensated by additional OH-/Cl- anions, and x-ray absorption detects no Cu1+, so it does not test doping of the kagome plane [104]. The chargon theory bears on these data only partly and over a limited composition range. The Li series extends to 1.81.8 Li per formula unit, 3/53/5 electron per Cu [71], well above both the densest commensurate endpoint x=1/6x=1/6 of the crystal ladder and the melting doping δ≈0.15\delta\approx 0.15 of the nearest-neighbor tt–JJ numerics above. Its insulating behavior in that upper range is left to the extrinsic dopant localization of Sec. VIII.1.

Doping a kagome DSL thus produces charge order instead of a large-Fermi-surface metal. At the mean-field level of Sec. VII.2, however, the condensate opens no insulating gap. Its electron-like quasiparticles form Fermi pockets of total Luttinger volume xx in all three states, and the condensate-induced gaps at the nodes lie 0.340.34 to 0.83​t0.83\,t away from the Fermi level. An insulator at the commensurate fillings therefore requires physics beyond mean field. The strong-coupling numerics above, which find insulating holon crystals [62, 102, 133], show that the tt–JJ model contains such physics. On that reading, insulation remains compatible with successful doping, since the tensor-network crystals survive with the sign of tt reversed, i.e. for electron doping [133]. Extrinsic localization remains possible [71]. In the weak-coupling itinerant limit the same layer disfavors a CDW [90], so the two limits bracket the observations.

VII.4 Transport and finite-temperature phenomenology

The transport predictions of the FL∗ framework [14, 9] carry over, subject to the two assumptions flagged in Sec. VII.1. While the chargons are uncondensed, the Hall number counts the doped density pp, the Luttinger volume of the pockets (3​p3p holes per three-site cell). A conventional Fermi liquid at the same doping would instead count the large Fermi surface of the half-filled middle band, 1+3​p1+3p holes per cell (the one-band value 1+p1+p does not apply to kagome). Throughout, Hall numbers are meant in the relaxation-time sense. The quantity nH=1/(e​RH)n_{H}=1/(eR_{H}) measures a carrier count only for pockets of a single sign with comparable mobilities, because the weak-field Hall conductivity is a property of the scattering-path geometry and not of the carrier density alone [98]. Anisotropy, variation of the scattering time over the pockets, and symmetry-allowed anomalous terms all loosen the identification. Within these limits the Hall number, invoked in Sec. VII.3, separates the large-Fermi-surface metal from both fractionalized states.

Beyond the Higgs transition the condensed phase is the chargon Higgs phase of Sec. VII.2, with the diagonal U(1) QEM−QgQ_{\rm EM}-Q_{g} unbroken and no reconstruction to a large-Fermi-surface metal. At mean field its electron-like quasiparticles form Fermi pockets of one carrier sign and total Luttinger volume pp around the two shifted Dirac nodes, in all three condensates (Sec. VII.2). On the same reading, the Hall number of the Higgs phase therefore counts pp, as in the FL∗, but for a band-structure reason. The parent’s Dirac nodes sit at half filling, so at electron density 1−p1-p the quasiparticle Fermi surface consists of pockets of volume pp rather than a large Fermi surface.

The Higgs phase and the FL∗ thus have the same Luttinger count and differ in translational order and in the condensate scale TρT_{\rho} (Sec. VIII). Nor is any Hall-number reconstruction toward the large-Fermi-surface count implied, because the doped charge resides in the condensate and an insulating state at the commensurate lock-ins requires physics beyond the quadratic spinon problem (Secs. VII.2 and VII.3). Above the ordering temperature, thermal chargon fluctuations produce arc-like spectral weight of the pseudogap type [9].

On kagome the leading finite-temperature scale is that of the condensate amplitude, TρT_{\rho}, which lies above any superconducting scale. For the gauge-charged condensate this scale marks a crossover and no true transition (Sec. VIII). Below it the MM-star charge order sets in at TCOT_{\rm CO}, and no Landau cubic forces this transition to be first order (Sec. III.2). Where superconductivity arises through a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} channel, it follows at or below TρT_{\rho}. The electromagnetic stiffness of a condensate built from a chargon condensate and paired spinons is the series (Ioffe–Larkin) combination of the two stiffnesses [80], so Tc≤TρT_{c}\leq T_{\rho}. Here TcT_{c} is set by the smaller of TρT_{\rho} and a spinon-pair scale TλT_{\lambda} proportional to the Higgs amplitude λ\lambda, which the theory does not fix (Sec. VIII).

A doped kagome DSL should therefore show the condensate scale TρT_{\rho} at or above the superconducting one, as the counterpart of the hierarchy TCO≫TcT_{\rm CO}\gg T_{c} of the kagome metals [24]. The inequality Tρ≥TcT_{\rho}\geq T_{c} follows from the Ioffe–Larkin combination once the lifted τ3\tau^{3} degeneracy provides a chargon stiffness, although the band structure alone does not fix the transition temperature that this stiffness sets. The inequality TCO<TρT_{\rm CO}<T_{\rho} depends on the octic anisotropy, the interlayer coupling and fluctuations (Sec. VIII). The full sequence is thus suggested by the ordering of scales but is not derived, and the position of TcT_{c} relative to TCOT_{\rm CO} depends on TλT_{\lambda}.

The charge order in this window is vestigial in the usual sense: a composite of the chargon multiplet orders over a range where the superconducting component does not. Unlike the usual scenario, the ordering Tρ≥TcT_{\rho}\geq T_{c} is derived here from the Ioffe–Larkin combination of the two stiffnesses, on the premise stated above.

Throughout, TCOT_{\rm CO} denotes the discrete lattice-symmetry-breaking transition of the charge order. It lies below the bare stiffness scale TρT_{\rho} of the condensate and is not fixed by tt and xx alone. Section VIII separates the two scales and gives the range of TρT_{\rho}.

VIII Discussion: experimental signatures

We fix units once, here, for herbertsmithite. We take the exchange J≃180J\simeq 180 K of ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2, the ab initio value [59] quoted in Ref. [97]. Experimental estimates run to 1717 meV ≃197\simeq 197 K, a 5%5\% shift that the UU range below absorbs. With J=4​tc2/UJ=4t_{c}^{2}/U for an effective one-band Hubbard UU of 33 to 55 eV, the electron hopping is |tc|=108|t_{c}|=108 to 139139 meV. The absolute scales of this section may be too low by a factor of order two. The 55 to 77 eV of the single-band fits of Ref. [90] and the 66 eV at which Ref. [59] obtains J1=182J_{1}=182 K would raise the electron hopping to 139139 to 165165 meV. The direct density-functional hopping of about 0.30.3 eV [90] lies higher still, and with it J=4​t2/UJ=4t^{2}/U overshoots the measured exchange several-fold. The chargon hopping is tB=2​c1​|tc|=48t_{B}=2c_{1}|t_{c}|=48 to 6262 meV at the mean-field level of Sec. II.1, where c1=0.221c_{1}=0.221 is the nearest-neighbor spinon bond amplitude of Sec. II.3. The spinon hopping is a different and much smaller quantity, tsp≃c1​J=3.4t_{\rm sp}\simeq c_{1}J=3.4 meV. At fixed JJ this gives tsp/tB=0.056t_{\rm sp}/t_{B}=0.056 to 0.0720.072 and |tc|/tsp=32|t_{c}|/t_{\rm sp}=32 to 4141.

Each quantity below is set by the hopping that appears in its own energy denominators. The chargon potential and its sextic and octic terms are set by tBt_{B}, the spinon-sea and spinon-polarization responses by tspt_{\rm sp}, and the matrix elements that couple the sectors by tct_{c}. We quote every chargon scale as a range, from its value at tBt_{B} to its value at the bare |tc||t_{c}|, which is an upper bound. Neither end captures the strong-coupling renormalization of the holon bandwidth (Sec. VII.3). The chargon flat-band gap of Sec. II.3 is then Δflat=(6−1)​tB=69\Delta_{\rm flat}=(\sqrt{6}-1)t_{B}=69 to 201201 meV (6969 to 8989 meV for tBt_{B}, 157157 to 201201 meV for the bare |tc||t_{c}|).

The bare phase-stiffness energy of the mean-field condensate defines the temperature TρT_{\rho}. With the isotropic valley curvature t/(2​6)t/(2\sqrt{6}) of Sec. II.3 and an areal chargon density of xx per site, kB​Tρ≃(π/2)​ℏ2​n/m∗=1.11​t​xk_{B}T_{\rho}\simeq(\pi/2)\,\hbar^{2}n/m^{*}=1.11\,tx, which runs from 1717 to 298298 K for x=1/36x=1/36 to 1/61/6 (1717 to 132132 K for the mean-field tBt_{B}). The Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless prefactor serves here as a normalization, and no phase transition is associated with this scale itself. Because B−B_{-} carries the emergent gauge charge, its phase is not gauge invariant. In the Higgs phase the gauge field absorbs it, leaving no Goldstone mode, no superfluid stiffness and no Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition. TρT_{\rho} marks the crossover below which the condensate amplitude, and with it the Higgs photon mass, is established and the composites of Table 2 become the slow variables. It estimates the condensate scale and bounds no ordering temperature.

The MM-star (or K/2K/2-star) charge order sets in at a discrete lattice-symmetry-breaking transition TCOT_{\rm CO}, which is not fixed by tt and xx alone. Because the pair sphere is degenerate through sextic order, the discrete orbit is selected by the octic anisotropy of Sec. IV.2, by interlayer coupling and by fluctuations. We expect TCOT_{\rm CO} below TρT_{\rho}, although we neither derive that ordering nor compute the scale. If the B2′B_{2}^{\prime} flux is ordered throughout the upper stage described below, as symmetry allows, the trilinear of Eq. (29) mixes the MM-point charge and current triplets linearly, and the charge order and the loop-current order set in together at TCOT_{\rm CO}, in a single transition.

The octic anisotropy sets one more scale. Its splitting per site between the stripe and triple-MM orbits, δ​e=0.351​(U​x/t)3​x​t\delta e=0.351\,(Ux/t)^{3}\,xt for on-site repulsion alone [Eq. (23)], is extensive. It becomes thermodynamically decisive only on patches of more than kB​T/δ​ek_{B}T/\delta e sites, that is, beyond a crossover length of order ℓ∗=kB​T/(δ​e​ns)=a​kB​T/(2​3​δ​e)\ell^{*}=\sqrt{k_{B}T/(\delta e\,n_{s})}=a\sqrt{k_{B}T/(2\sqrt{3}\,\delta e)}, with ns=2​3/a2n_{s}=2\sqrt{3}/a^{2} the kagome site density used for TρT_{\rho} above. Below ℓ∗\ell^{*} the choice between the two orbits is thermally undetermined. Since δ​e\delta e falls as x4x^{4}, ℓ∗\ell^{*} grows rapidly toward the dilute end.

For the illustrative choice U=tU=t, two orders of magnitude below the charging-energy scale of Sec. IV.1 (UU is not derived here), δ​e\delta e stays below 0.50.5 K per site throughout x≤1/6x\leq 1/6, and ℓ∗\ell^{*} for T=2T=2 to 1010 K is one to three lattice constants at x=1/6x=1/6 and 280280 to 720720 Å (4040 to 105105 lattice constants, a=6.83a=6.83 Å) at x=1/36x=1/36. These are crossover lengths. A domain size would additionally require domain-wall and disorder energetics, which are beyond this work. At the physical charging energy the octic expansion behind δ​e\delta e is outside its range (Sec. IV.1), so these lengths illustrate the x4x^{4} scaling and do not predict a value.

These scales suggest a two-stage finite-temperature structure. Below TρT_{\rho} lies an upper stage in which the condensate has stiffness but the pair sphere is not yet resolved into a discrete orbit, so uni-MM and tri-MM correlations are short-ranged. The Γ\Gamma-point composites that are constant over the pair sphere, such as the B2′B_{2}^{\prime} staggered flux of Sec. IV.4, are then symmetry-allowed to order before the MM-triplet does, and the charge-ordering transition follows at TCOT_{\rm CO}. We do not derive this structure, and whether these composites actually order is a fluctuation question outside the present theory.

Superconductivity, where the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} channel allows it, lies at or below TρT_{\rho}. It requires both the chargon condensate and the spinon pairing. The electromagnetic phase stiffness of such a two-component condensate is the series (Ioffe–Larkin) combination ρEM=ρB​ρf/(ρB+ρf)\rho_{\rm EM}=\rho_{B}\rho_{f}/(\rho_{B}+\rho_{f}) [80] of the chargon stiffness ρB\rho_{B}, which sets TρT_{\rho}, and the stiffness ρf\rho_{f} of the paired spinons. The pair amplitude and the phase stiffness are distinct quantities, and with the spinon Fermi surface present at nf=1±xn_{f}=1\pm x the relation between them needs a separate response calculation. We assume that the spinon stiffness scales with the Higgs amplitude λ\lambda, with a coefficient of order unity that we do not compute. Then Tc≲min⁡(Tρ,Tλ)T_{c}\lesssim\min(T_{\rho},T_{\lambda}), where kB​Tλ∝λk_{B}T_{\lambda}\propto\lambda is an input of the theory.

The physical pair amplitude of Sec. V.2 is linear in λ\lambda and in the condensate density xx through the composite of Eq. (33) and, for α\alpha, β\beta and δ\delta, through the B+B_{+} admixture [amplitude per unit λ/t\lambda/t: 1/[2​(1+6)]=0.1451/[2(1+\sqrt{6})]=0.145 for the on-site channel of β\beta, 3/2\sqrt{3}/2 for α\alpha, 6/2\sqrt{6}/2 for δ\delta and zero for γ\gamma]. This order-parameter amplitude sets the size of the induced electron pair field and has no direct meaning as a temperature. The band structure provides the energy scale kB​Tρ=1.11​t​xk_{B}T_{\rho}=1.11\,tx against which λ\lambda may be compared, and for λ/t=0.05\lambda/t=0.05 to 0.30.3 and x=1/12x=1/12 to 1/61/6 the two are of the same order. The separation between TρT_{\rho} and TcT_{c} is therefore not parametric, and the band structure fixes neither TcT_{c} nor TρT_{\rho} as a transition temperature.

VIII.1 Doped spin-liquid materials: the intrinsic scenario

Herbertsmithite and its polymorphs remain the central kagome spin-liquid materials [97, 40], with inelastic neutron scattering now identifying universal spin excitations across the herbertsmithite and Zn-barlowite families [10]. Progress on the charge sector has been slower. Ga substitution was predicted to give a correlated Dirac metal at 1/31/3 doping [90], but in the realized series the Ga3+ charge is anion-compensated and the kagome plane is undoped [104]. The only electron-doped series realized so far, Li intercalation, in which photoemission sees Cu1+, remains insulating at every composition studied [71]. First-principles work attributes this to dopant-induced localization and polaron formation [85, 63].

The chargon theory adds an intrinsic mechanism, independent of dopant disorder. Even ideal, disorder-free doping of the kagome DSL is not expected to produce a conventional metal or a superconductor at leading order. It produces instead a charge-ordered chargon Higgs phase (Secs. IV, VII), in which the physical U⁡(1)U(1), the diagonal combination generated by the difference of the electromagnetic and gauge charges, remains unbroken.

With only B−B_{-} condensed, the electron is the condensate-weighted particle–hole conjugate of the spinon (Sec. II.1), and the condensate feeds back on the spinon hopping through the gauge-invariant bond amplitude B¯i​si​j​Bj\bar{B}_{i}s_{ij}B_{j} (Sec. VII). At the mean-field level of the quadratic spinon problem this feedback opens no Dirac mass at linear order in xx. At the Gauss-law filling nf=1∓xn_{f}=1\mp x the electron-like quasiparticles of all three condensates form Fermi pockets of total volume xx around the Dirac nodes. (For the electron-doped series of this section the spinons sit at nf=1−xn_{f}=1-x, with the Fermi level 0.430.43 to 1.35​t1.35\,t below the nodes.) An insulating gap at the commensurate fillings must therefore come from confinement, from interactions beyond the quadratic spinon problem, or from physics that, by the counting argument of Sec. VII.2, breaks a further symmetry or carries topological order. At mean field the condensate does not account for the insulating behavior of the realized doping series, and the present analysis does not settle whether the phase is insulating.

Translational order distinguishes intrinsic chargon crystallization from extrinsic localization, which produces no new translational order. Ordered dopants or a dopant-induced lattice distortion can, however, generate satellites independently, so observed satellites are compatible with both scenarios. Intrinsic chargon crystallization produces

  • •

    superlattice Bragg satellites at the charge-carrying composite stars of Table 2, MM (2×22\times 2 or stripe) and K/2K/2 (12×12\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12}, thirty-six-site), with commensurate fillings at x=1/36x=1/36, x=1/12x=1/12 and x=1/6x=1/6;

  • •

    a C2C_{2}-odd 2×22\times 2 pattern (Sec. III.2);

  • •

    a charge-ordering transition free of any symmetry-mandated first-order mechanism;

  • •

    loop-current magnetism whose MM-modulated part switches on at the same transition, visible to μ\muSR and, by symmetry, open to polar Kerr in its multi-arm realizations (triple-MM, K/2K/2) and closed to it in the uni-MM stripe (Sec. VIII.2).

The KK star is absent from the diffraction list because its site-density form factor and its gauge-invariant bond charge out to third-neighbor range vanish identically for every condensate, so the 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} channel is a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd loop-current crystal. Local magnetic probes can see it, whereas x-rays and electrons cannot.

Diffraction is the most direct test of the intrinsic scenario, and the modulation it must detect is small in absolute terms. For the phase-I stripe the site densities of the pure valley condensate take the three values x⁡(1∓1/2)x(1\mp 1/\sqrt{2}) and xx, each on one third of the sites. This gives a peak modulation δ​n=x/2=0.020\delta n=x/\sqrt{2}=0.020 to 0.1180.118 electrons per Cu for x=1/36x=1/36 to 1/61/6. The triple-MM state has δ​n=2/3​x\delta n=\sqrt{2/3}\,x, and the K/2K/2 crystal has δ​n=(1/2+1/(2​3))​x≃x\delta n=(1/\sqrt{2}+1/(2\sqrt{3}))\,x\simeq x.

The corresponding diffraction intensities are order-of-magnitude estimates. We compare with the total electron count per Cu of the host (68.368.3 for ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2, all atoms, with q→0q\to 0 atomic form factors, so that IBraggI_{\rm Bragg} is the strongest conceivable fundamental reflection). The purely electronic contribution to a superlattice reflection is then Isuper/IBragg=|δ​n/ntot|2≃10−7I_{\rm super}/I_{\rm Bragg}=|\delta n/n_{\rm tot}|^{2}\simeq 10^{-7} to 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} for the stripe over the same doping range. These figures are upper bounds, because the diffracted structure factor itself is the Fourier amplitude, 2​x/3\sqrt{2}\,x/3 at MM for the stripe and (1+2)​x/(6​3)=0.23​x(1+\sqrt{2})\,x/(6\sqrt{3})=0.23\,x per member of the K/2K/2 star. The structure-factor ratios are 4×10−84\times 10^{-8} to 1.3×10−61.3\times 10^{-6} for the stripe and 9×10−99\times 10^{-9} to 3×10−73\times 10^{-7} per K/2K/2 satellite. The estimate omits powder averaging, Debye–Waller factors and the interlayer structure of the crystal, and it assumes full condensation of the doped charge.

Imposing the site-resolved Gauss law cuts the modulation further, by a factor of 4444 at x=1/6x=1/6 in the lattice calculation of Appendix B. At x=1/36x=1/36, which for UB/tB=4U_{B}/t_{B}=4 alone lies inside the miscibility gap of Appendix B, the homogeneous state does not suppress the modulation but moves it to the longest wavelength the torus admits. Its root-mean-square contrast falls only by a factor of 1.21.2. Both factors are root-mean-square contrasts at one set of parameters, and the spatial pattern changes between the two states. They rescale the summed Fourier power and not any individual satellite, and correcting a specific intensity would need a mode-resolved calculation. The orbital fields of the following subsection are reduced as well, by the smaller factors 1.41.4 and 7.07.0 at the same two dopings.

The accompanying lattice distortion, which dominates the satellite intensity in known charge-density-wave systems, requires an electron–phonon coupling that the chargon theory does not contain, and we have no estimate of its size. The electronic channel alone is a demanding target for x-ray diffraction, so the test falls first to probes that see the electronic modulation directly, that is, electron diffraction and scanned probes (tunneling where a surface conducts, noncontact force microscopy otherwise). Synchrotron x-ray diffraction regains its advantage if the lattice channel is appreciable.

The natural x-ray probe of an electronic modulation of this size in a copper compound is resonant scattering at the Cu L3L_{3} edge, where the amplitude is dominated by the 3​d3d valence and where charge orders of comparable amplitude are measured in the cuprates [19]. A modulation δ​n\delta n of the 3​d3d occupancy then gives a resonant superlattice contrast of order δ​n2\delta n^{2} if the resonant form factor follows the occupancy linearly, i.e. 4×10−44\times 10^{-4} to 10−210^{-2} for the δ​n=0.02\delta n=0.02 to 0.120.12 per Cu of the stripe, against the 10−710^{-7} of the non-resonant estimate. Both stars are within reach at the edge (|M|=0.53|M|=0.53 Å-1 and |K/2|=0.31|K/2|=0.31 Å-1 against 2​k=0.942k=0.94 Å-1 at 930930 eV), and the resonant channel separates the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-even charge composites (F3F_{3}) from the current composites (F2′F_{2}^{\prime}). Neither contrast figure is a bound. The resonant one assumes a sensitivity that we have not calibrated, since the contrast depends on the occupancy derivative of the complex resonant form factor, on photon energy and polarization, and on the reference reflection, and energy-dependent complex amplitudes and interference can suppress the contrast as well as enhance it.

The K/2K/2 target is the six-fold star {(13,16),(16,13),(−16,16),(−13,−16),(−16,−13),(16,−16)}\{(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{6}),(\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{3}),(-\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{6}),(-\tfrac{1}{3},-\tfrac{1}{6}),(-\tfrac{1}{6},-\tfrac{1}{3}),(\tfrac{1}{6},-\tfrac{1}{6})\} in reciprocal-lattice units of the kagome cell, with the 60∘60^{\circ} axes 𝐚1=(1,0)\mathbf{a}_{1}=(1,0), 𝐚2=(12,32)\mathbf{a}_{2}=(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) of Appendix A. In the standard hexagonal setting of R​3¯​mR\bar{3}m herbertsmithite, γ=120∘\gamma=120^{\circ}, the same star is (16,16,l)(\tfrac{1}{6},\tfrac{1}{6},l) and its symmetry equivalents, half of K=(13,13,0)K=(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},0). Its members have |q|=2​π/3​a=|K|/2|q|=2\pi/3a=|K|/2 along Γ\Gamma-KK (0.310.31 Å-1 for a=6.83a=6.83 Å) and are reciprocal-lattice vectors of the 12×12\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12} (R​30∘R30^{\circ}) cell. The K/2K/2 crystal carries no MM or KK charge component (its MM- and KK-star weight is loop current, Sec. IV.3), and the out-of-plane index is not fixed by the single-layer theory. The MM-star satellites of the stripe are extinguished by the intra-cell structure factor in every second zone.

Absence of any satellite on either star, in a cleanly doped sample and at a sensitivity reaching the estimates above, would exclude the fixed-parent crystals computed here at that doping, while a less sensitive null constrains the unestimated lattice channel alone. A sensitive null would still leave the intrinsic chargon mechanism as such open, since the parent flux pattern is itself expected to collapse above the x∗x^{*} of Sec. VII.3, which lies below the dopings at issue.

The prediction can be tested on the Li-intercalated series [71]. To our knowledge no superlattice reflection has been reported for it, and it remains to be checked whether its structural characterization is sensitive enough to reach the electronic estimate. The test concerns the dilute end of that series, at and below the densest commensurate filling x=1/6x=1/6. Its upper range, which reaches 3/53/5 electron per Cu, lies beyond every commensurate filling and beyond the melting doping of the tt–JJ numerics (Sec. VII.3), and falls to the extrinsic scenario.

Pressure is a complementary control parameter for the parent magnet. Y-kapellasite, which orders magnetically at ambient pressure, loses its static magnetism under hydrostatic pressure and is fully fluctuating at 2.32.3 GPa as the anisotropy of its kagome lattice is reduced [13]. Pressure can therefore tune a clean kagome magnet toward the spin-liquid regime. The experiment has no charge-sector content, since the compound is undoped, and it does not bear on the crystallize-or-condense alternative posed here. The same alternative arises for the doped cluster-Mott spin-liquid candidate 1T-TaS2, where gate doping of thin samples has been proposed to evade dopant localization [78].

In ultracold atoms the dispersive chargon problem is realizable in principle with artificial gauge fields, by the optically induced staggered fluxes of Ref. [96] or the laser-controlled tunneling phases discussed for kagome optical lattices in Ref. [48]. The emulator would be bosons hopping on the kagome lattice with the Bloch matrix −t​M​(𝐤)-t\,M(\mathbf{k}) of Sec. II.2, in the [0,π][0,\pi] sign pattern and with the sign of tt that places the flat multiplet at the top of the spectrum, at +2​t+2t, and the four isotropic, nondegenerate minima at −(1+6)​t-(1+\sqrt{6})t.

Such an emulator can test the leading selection of Sec. IV.1, together with the density and current patterns of the selected states. Whether the condensate occupies one translation pair or both, i.e. MM-star against K/2K/2-star order, is set by the intersite repulsion measured against the crossover Vc≃9.3​U2​x/tV_{c}\simeq 9.3\,U^{2}x/t of Eq. (22) and, for purely on-site interactions at small xx, by the two-boson (ladder) correction to the projected quartic. This correction does not lie on the Hubbard ray. It contributes EI−EII−=−0.053U2x2/tE_{\rm I}-E_{\rm II^{-}}=-0.053\,U^{2}x^{2}/t per site and selects the MM star below x≃0.036x\simeq 0.036.

The octic lifting of the pair sphere is out of reach. Wherever the expansion of Eq. (23) is controlled, the splitting of the uni-MM and triple-MM orbits is smaller than the quartic energy by the factor 0.263​ϵB20.263\,\epsilon_{B}^{2}, with ϵB=U​ρ¯/tB\epsilon_{B}=U\bar{\rho}/t_{B} at filling ρ¯\bar{\rho} per site. An emulator also carries neither the emergent gauge field nor the B+B_{+} sector. Its condensate is an ordinary superfluid carrying the density and current patterns of Sec. IV without the Higgs structure, and nothing of the pairing analysis of Sec. V transfers to it.

VIII.2 Fingerprints of the chargon orders

Charge sector. The charge order is 2×22\times 2 or stripe, with an F3F_{3} (C2C_{2}-odd) MM-triplet. It has no cubic invariant, hence no symmetry-mandated first-order transition, and its TrH-like and SoD-like registries are exactly degenerate. The C2C_{2} parity holds at every order for the uni-MM stripe, and up to an F1F_{1} admixture of relative order U​x/tUx/t for the triple-MM state (Sec. III.2). Scanning tunneling microscopy needs a conducting surface, which the insulating doped materials realized so far do not offer. The parity must therefore be read from diffraction, through the zone-to-zone intensity ratios and extinctions of the MM-star satellites, or from noncontact force microscopy, which images lattice and charge modulations on insulating surfaces. The uni-MM/tri-MM landscape is soft. It is split only at octic order, by 1/57=1.75%1/57=1.75\% of the octic moment and by 0.351​(U​x/t)3​x​t0.351\,(Ux/t)^{3}\,xt per site in the derived octic [Eq. (23)]. The selected pattern should be extremely sensitive to strain and disorder, and the stripe should form three 120∘120^{\circ} domain families.

Current sector. The currents are staggered triangle loop currents. Their MM-modulated part switches on at TCOT_{\rm CO}, while the Γ\Gamma-point part is symmetry-allowed to set in already in the upper stage described at the head of this section. For the uni-MM stripe the circulations are 32​(3−2)∓12​(3−6)={0.2015, 0.7520}​t​ρ¯\tfrac{3}{2}(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})\mp\tfrac{1}{2}(3-\sqrt{6})=\{0.2015,\,0.7520\}\,t\bar{\rho} on up-triangles and opposite on down-triangles, in the convention Ji​j=2​Im​[B¯i​si​j​Bj]J_{ij}=2\,\mathrm{Im}[\bar{B}_{i}s_{ij}B_{j}] of the Fig. 5 caption, with ρ¯\bar{\rho} the mean chargon site density. The pattern is the sum of a Γ\Gamma-point B2′B_{2}^{\prime} staggered flux and an F2′F_{2}^{\prime} modulation at the activated MM points. The flux is 32​(3−2)​t​ρ¯\tfrac{3}{2}(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})\,t\bar{\rho} per up-triangle on average and is saturated by every phase-I condensate (|Δ​N|=∑ηnη|\Delta N|=\sum_{\eta}n_{\eta} over the whole moduli sphere). The modulation has amplitude 12​(3−6)​t​ρ¯\tfrac{1}{2}(3-\sqrt{6})\,t\bar{\rho} for the single-arm stripe, smaller by a factor of 3\sqrt{3}.

For the uni-MM stripe both parts carry zero net moment, which its unitary glide mirror enforces. Local probes (μ\muSR, NMR line broadening) and polarized neutron diffraction see them, but the uniform response functions (polar Kerr, zero-field anomalous Hall), which transform as A2′A_{2}^{\prime}, do not. The triple-MM state and the K/2K/2 crystal are not so protected (magnetic classes 3​m′3m^{\prime} and 6​m′​m′6m^{\prime}m^{\prime}, Sec. IV.2). Their three current arms form the A2′A_{2}^{\prime} composite Δ1′​Δ2′​Δ3′\Delta_{1}^{\prime}\Delta_{2}^{\prime}\Delta_{3}^{\prime}, so a Kerr or Hall signal is symmetry-allowed there, cubic in the current bilinears and hence of order x3x^{3}. The uniform responses discriminate the uni-MM stripe from the multi-arm states.

The local fields below are order-of-magnitude, single-layer, mean-field estimates for a stated geometry, and they vary from site to site. They assume full condensation (ρ¯=x\bar{\rho}=x), treat the bond currents as classical line currents, and fix the sign pattern only up to the overall sense of circulation. The current that enters them is that of the frozen link field of the undoped ansatz, and the numbers are not evaluated at a jointly stationary, constraint-consistent saddle. The feedback-dressed χi​j​(B)\chi_{ij}(B) of Sec. VII.2 corrects them at relative order tc​x/tspt_{c}x/t_{\rm sp}, which is of order one over the doping window (Sec. VII.2).

With Ii​j=e​Ji​jI_{ij}=eJ_{ij}, Ji​j=2​Im​[B¯i​si​j​Bj]​t​ρ¯/ℏJ_{ij}=2\,\mathrm{Im}[\bar{B}_{i}s_{ij}B_{j}]\,t\bar{\rho}/\hbar (the Heisenberg current of the hopping Hamiltonian) and ρ¯=x\bar{\rho}=x, the largest bond current of the uni-MM stripe is 0.884​e​t​x/ℏ≃0.60.884\,etx/\hbar\simeq 0.6 to 5​μ5\,\muA for the bare t=|tc|=108t=|t_{c}|=108 to 139139 meV and x=1/36x=1/36 to 1/61/6 (0.30.3 to 2​μ2\,\muA for t=tBt=t_{B}). Currents and fields scale linearly with tt. The site values below are for the bare |tc||t_{c}| and are smaller by the factor tB/|tc|=0.44t_{B}/|t_{c}|=0.44 at the mean-field chargon hopping tBt_{B}.

Biot–Savart integration over the bond currents of the periodically repeated 12×1212\times 12 torus, treating each bond as a straight segment of length a/2=3.42a/2=3.42 Å (with a=6.83a=6.83 Å for herbertsmithite), gives a site-dependent orbital field that scales as B≃10​(36​x)​(t/108​meV)B\simeq 10\,(36x)\,(t/108\,{\rm meV}) G. In the kagome plane the field is normal to the plane. It is 1010 to 1313 G at a hexagon center and 66 to 99 G at a triangle center for x=1/36x=1/36, rising to 6060 to 7777 G and 3535 to 5555 G at x=1/6x=1/6, with opposite sign on the two hexagons of the doubled cell and on up- and down-triangles. At 1.51.5 Å above a triangle center, a plausible muon site, it is 66 to 99 G at x=1/36x=1/36 and 3939 to 5555 G at x=1/6x=1/6, mostly in-plane there. It falls to about half by 33 Å and to a tenth by 55 to 66 Å above the plane.

Over all sites within 33 Å of the plane the range is 33 to 2020 G at x=1/36x=1/36 and 1818 to 118118 G at x=1/6x=1/6, that is 0.040.04 to 1.61.6 MHz of muon precession, one to three orders of magnitude above the characteristic fields reported by zero-field μ\muSR at the charge-order transitions of the kagome metals, which range from about 0.10.1 G (CsV3Sb5, a zero-field relaxation-rate step of 0.0075​μ​s−10.0075~\mu{\rm s}^{-1} at TCDWT_{\rm CDW} [72]) to 0.30.3 G (KV3Sb5 [95]).

In herbertsmithite the muon binds to a hydroxyl group, the OH–μ\mu complex identified by zero-field μ\muSR [92] (with a minority Cl site), at about 11 Å from the hydroxyl O in an unrefined direction. Over the possible directions the field is 66 to 1616 G at x=1/36x=1/36 and 3535 to 9898 G at x=1/6x=1/6, and the height scan brackets the Cl site and other choices.

The two NMR ligand nuclei of herbertsmithite, 17O and 35Cl, sit off the current paths and can be estimated the same way. The 17O of the hydroxyl bridging each Cu–Cu bond sits 0.860.86 Å out of the plane and 0.530.53 Å in-plane from the bond midpoint toward the adjacent hexagon center (1.01.0 Å from the midpoint; Cu–O 1.981.98 Å, Cu–O–Cu 119∘119^{\circ}, Cu–Cu 3.423.42 Å [113]), where the field is 1111 to 2020 G at x=1/36x=1/36 and 6565 to 118118 G at x=1/6x=1/6. The 35Cl caps each Cu3 triangle on its threefold axis 1.941.94 Å above the triangle center (Cu–Cl 2.772.77 Å [113]), where it is 55 to 77 G and 3131 to 4444 G (all ranges, here and above, over the tt interval and the inequivalent members of the doubled cell). The Cu nucleus sits on the current paths. Its orbital hyperfine field requires the current density within the 3​d3d shell, not line currents, so we quote no number for it.

The site densities also leave a signature at the Cu nucleus that needs no current estimate. Through the change of the electric-field gradient with the 3​d3d occupancy, and following the density levels and multiplicities of Secs. IV.2 and IV.3, the inequivalent sites of each crystal split the 63,65Cu nuclear quadrupole resonance line generically into

  • •

    three lines of equal weight (1:1:11{:}1{:}1) for the stripe;

  • •

    three lines of weights 1:2:11{:}2{:}1 for the triple-MM state;

  • •

    five lines of weights 1:1:2:1:11{:}1{:}2{:}1{:}1 for the K/2K/2 crystal,

with the corresponding 17O and 35Cl splittings set by the bond and triangle densities. The NQR line multiplicity settled the charge-order pattern in CsV3Sb5 [65]. The multiplicities listed are idealized and can err in either direction. Equal density need not mean equal gradient, which can raise the multiplicity, while an accidental coincidence of gradients at inequivalent densities, or disorder broadening, can lower the resolved count. An estimate of the size of the splitting would require the gradient per unit occupancy.

The Cu2+ paramagnetic and nuclear-dipolar background of herbertsmithite is of comparable magnitude, but its static electronic part is small. The same zero-field μ\muSR experiment bounds any static electronic field at the muon site of the undoped compound at about 0.30.3 G [92]. The nuclear-dipolar part is static but temperature-independent, so it does not switch on at a transition. The discriminating signal is therefore a static component whose line shape switches on at TCOT_{\rm CO} (or, for the Γ\Gamma-point part, in the upper stage), whatever its size.

A magnetic field couples the F3F_{3} charge order linearly to the F4′F_{4}^{\prime} flux channel, the 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd MM-triplet that is odd under both C2C_{2} and σv\sigma_{v} (the product of F3F_{3} with the A2′A_{2}^{\prime} of the field, and not F2′F_{2}^{\prime}) [24]. No term linear in the field and in F3F_{3} therefore selects the sense of circulation of the F2′F_{2}^{\prime} currents, so the field-training protocols of the F1F_{1} kagome metals do not apply through the charge order, and domain-selective protocols remain. Uniaxial strain selects one of the three F3F_{3} stripe orientations and with it the momentum of the accompanying F2′F_{2}^{\prime} arm. Polarized neutron diffraction, at the nuclear Bragg positions for the Γ\Gamma-point B2′B_{2}^{\prime} flux and at the MM and KK stars for the modulated parts, detects the staggered orbital moments without training.

Pair sector. Superconductivity, when present, is a pair-density wave on the phase-I and II- arcs, with no uniform charge-2​e2e component at the quartic level. Phase I carries K/2K/2-star modulations alone (period 3 along Γ\Gamma-KK, 12×12​R​30∘\sqrt{12}\times\sqrt{12}\,R30^{\circ}), and branch II- carries these together with MM-star (period-2) modulations, both with the descendant-resolved irreps of Table 4. A first-harmonic (sin⁡ϕ\sin\phi) Josephson null against a conventional lead is the classic pair-density-wave diagnostic [1]. Because disorder, strain, surfaces and domain averaging all generate a uniform component, a null is interpreted relative to a control junction on a uniform superconductor.

The positive test is the charge of the lowest uniform pair composite (Sec. V.3). The II- crystal has a second-harmonic (sin⁡2​ϕ\sin 2\phi) Josephson coupling and an h/4​eh/4e flux period of the vestigial phase, the triple-MM state has an h/6​eh/6e period, and the uni-MM stripe has no low-order uniform pair channel at all. The pairing channels are the A1A_{1}/B1B_{1}/B2B_{2}/A2A_{2} assignments of Sec. V.3. The vortex and edge features quoted there correspond to them channel by channel and are not computed spectra. The channels carry no uniform d+i​dd+id at leading order, nor at any order on the MM-star condensates.

VIII.3 Kagome metals: convergences and discriminators

The kagome metals lie outside the regime of this theory. Their CDWs are F1F_{1}-type, weakly first order, with substantial phonon involvement [24]. The orders of the metals and of the doped insulator are nevertheless classified by the same space-group irreducible representations, and recent experiments make the comparison concrete.

In weak-coupling theory, sublattice interference suppresses all conventional weak-coupling instabilities [73], renders the local repulsion irrelevant and, in a large-VV model at intermediate coupling, promotes MM-point pair-density waves without uniform superconductivity [130]. It also leads to MM-star loop-current order whose Landau trilinear vanishes [34, 138]. That order and the loop currents that the strong-coupling chargon theory derives (Secs. IV.4, IV.2) both transform in the F2′F_{2}^{\prime} channel, with the same cubic-free structure. Chargons in the doped spin liquid and electrons in the kagome metals thus both prefer finite-momentum pairing. Whether the spinons of the undoped magnet do as well, as the proposed spinon pair-density wave would imply [143], is unsettled, since its variational energies have been challenged as a sampling artifact [67]. The recent developments below can be read in chargon-theoretic terms, although shared irreps do not imply shared mechanisms.

(i) Inversion-breaking charge order. Combined STM/nc-AFM/SHG on the AAV3Sb5 family finds that in-plane inversion symmetry is spontaneously broken in the 2×22\times 2 CDW state. The authors report a mixed-parity order with ferro-polar (dipolar) and nematic (quadrupolar) moments whose coupling produces an electronic chirality [111]. Its ferro-polar (Γ\Gamma-point E1E_{1}) and chiral components appear nowhere in Table 2. The inversion-odd MM-point part of such a state lies in the C2C_{2}-odd site-density channel F3F_{3} or F4F_{4}, mixed with F1F_{1}. These two differ only in mirror character, which is not reported. The chargon mechanism populates F3F_{3} directly, whereas in the weak-coupling theories it appears as an induced subsidiary order. (Bulk NQR on hole-doped CsV3Sb5-xSnx still fits the staggered trihexagonal F1F_{1} state [65].)

Site-selective 121Sb NQR on CsV3Sb5 resolves a magnetic line broadening below T∗≃120T^{*}\simeq 120 K, consistent with spontaneous local fields of order 11 mT from loop currents [120]. The authors tie that onset to the nematic transition above TCDW≃94T_{\rm CDW}\simeq 94 K. Staggered fields that precede the charge order are what the upper stage of Sec. VIII would permit, with Γ\Gamma-point B2′B_{2}^{\prime} flux and E2E_{2} nematic composites symmetry-allowed to order before the MM triplet. The same material has a null polar Kerr response below the charge-order transition [108]. A 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd order with no net moment, visible to a local probe and invisible to σx​y\sigma_{xy}, has the symmetry of the staggered B2′B_{2}^{\prime} and F2′F_{2}^{\prime} channels of Table 2 in their single-arm (uni-MM) realization, whose unitary glide mirror forbids the A2′A_{2}^{\prime} composite that three arms would form. The observation agrees with the symmetry classification of (iii) below, while the quantitative test of the present currents remains the local-field estimate of Sec. VIII.2 for doped herbertsmithite.

(ii) Softness of the charge-order landscape. In CsV3-xTixSb5, Ti substitution as dilute as x=0.009x=0.009 suppresses the three-dimensional 2×2×42\times 2\times 4 CDW of the pristine compound and reduces the remaining 2×2×22\times 2\times 2 order to a quasi-two-dimensional one. By x=0.2x=0.2 x-ray diffraction and STM find instead a (quasi-)one-dimensional stripe CDW with a correlation length of only ∼20\sim\!20 Å, whose intensity and correlation length grow continuously below ∼56\sim\!56 K as at a second-order transition [131]. Short-range nematic domains outlive the long-range CDW entirely [132]. Neither observation tests the present theory, whose charge order is F3F_{3} while that of the metals is F1F_{1}. They show that a stripe channel and a second-order-like onset are available on the kagome lattice once the first-order mechanism of the pristine F1F_{1} order is disrupted, as they would be for the cubic-free F3F_{3} transition and the uni-MM/tri-MM near-degeneracy described here.

(iii) TRSB channel selection. High-resolution Sagnac interferometry finds no spontaneous Kerr rotation in CsV3Sb5 and ScV6Sn6 down to a noise floor below ∼100\sim\!100 nrad, including under strain [108]. Meanwhile μ\muSR reports time-reversal breaking at the CDW in KV3Sb5 [95] and in CsV3Sb5 itself [72, 137], and circular-dichroism ARPES reports it well above the CDW transition [12]. Staggered flux orders with zero net moment reconcile the two sets of observations, and the uni-MM stripe of phase I carries such orders. Its Γ\Gamma-point B2′B_{2}^{\prime} flux and its single activated F2′F_{2}^{\prime} arm are both staggered. Neither couples linearly to σx​y\sigma_{xy}, which transforms as the pseudoscalar A2′A_{2}^{\prime} (C2C_{2}-even, mirror-odd, 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd), and the stripe’s unitary glide mirror forbids any A2′A_{2}^{\prime} component.

The Kerr null is consistent with the uni-MM stripe, and it constrains the multi-arm states. The triple-MM state (3​m′3m^{\prime}) and the K/2K/2 crystal (6​m′​m′6m^{\prime}m^{\prime}) carry the A2′A_{2}^{\prime} composite Δ1′​Δ2′​Δ3′\Delta_{1}^{\prime}\Delta_{2}^{\prime}\Delta_{3}^{\prime} of their three current arms, which is absent from Table 2 only because that table lists bilinears. A Kerr rotation of order x3x^{3} is symmetry-allowed in both, with a size that the present theory does not fix.

(iv) An intrinsic pair-density wave. Following the original STM observation of a 4​a3\frac{4a}{3} “roton” pair modulation [16], phase-sensitive tunneling in KV3Sb5, read through Ginzburg–Landau theory, supports a sign-changing MM-star PDW that is primary and not induced [135] (Sec. V.3). STM finds a field-trainable chiral 2×22\times 2 pair modulation, interpreted as a pair-density wave of the vanadium dd-orbital sector, with the uniform pairing carried by the Sb pp-orbital sector [115]. Ring interferometry shows π\pi-shifted Little–Parks oscillations in nearly every device [125], indicating a sign-changing multicomponent condensate. Between the π\pi- and 00-phase regimes it also shows h/4​eh/4e-periodic oscillations, which the authors attribute to a second-harmonic crossover between a dominant sign-changing and a subdominant uniform component and not to charge-4​e4e order.

In both materials a substantial uniform pair component coexists with the modulation. The pure pair-density-wave arcs of the descendants, with no uniform charge-2​e2e component at the quartic level, are not realized there, and the agreement is confined to the MM-star irrep classification of the modulated part. The topological-PDW scenario requires the MM pair triplet to induce a uniform d+i​dd+id component at third order [136]. The same analysis expects that component to be so small that the state is effectively gapless, with Bogoliubov Fermi surfaces, at accessible temperatures. An F3F_{3} pair triplet forbids this cubic, so its Bogoliubov Fermi surfaces would be symmetry-enforced instead of approximate. Since the two cases look alike to spectroscopy, the discriminator between an F1F_{1}-type and an F3F_{3}-type pair multiplet is the C2C_{2} parity of the triplet itself, or the presence or absence of any Q=0Q=0 pair component in a phase-sensitive (Josephson) measurement. For the descendants’ own MM-star condensates no uniform component arises at any order, while on the K/2K/2 branch one is induced at the next order (Sec. V.3).

(v) The KK and K/2K/2 stars. The C3C_{3}-symmetric 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} CDW of ScV6Sn6 is a KK-point charge order, which the chargon KK channel does not produce. Its site-density form factor and its bond charge out to third-neighbor range vanish identically (Sec. IV.4), and it carries instead a 𝒯\mathcal{T}-odd 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} loop-current crystal. Superconducting CeRu3Si2 adds a case whose μ\muSR-only time-reversal breaking remains compatible with a current-carrying PDW in place of d+i​dd+id. It has dual flat bands, a dominant MM-star charge order and a weak period-3 order. The satellites of the latter appear at (13,13,l)(\tfrac{1}{3},\tfrac{1}{3},l)-type positions, but the order is assigned to three single-qq orthorhombic (I​m​m​aImma) domains and not to a KK-point order [35].

The K/2K/2 star remains the open channel. The unidirectional period-4​a4a stripe seen by STM in CsV3Sb5 [140, 16] sits at one quarter of a reciprocal-lattice vector, (14,0)(\tfrac{1}{4},0) in the reciprocal-lattice units of Sec. VIII.1 and (14,−14)(\tfrac{1}{4},-\tfrac{1}{4}) in the R​3¯​mR\bar{3}m setting, along Γ\Gamma-MM in both. Its wavevector, of length π/(3​a)\pi/(\sqrt{3}\,a), is 13.4%13.4\% shorter than |K/2|=2​π/(3​a)|K/2|=2\pi/(3a) and rotated by 30∘30^{\circ} from the Γ\Gamma-KK directions of the K/2K/2 star, so the stripe is not a K/2K/2 order. Its wavelength 2​3​a=3.46​a2\sqrt{3}\,a=3.46a, the 4​a4a repeat along the lattice row times cos⁡30∘\cos 30^{\circ}, is correspondingly 15.5%15.5\% longer than the 3​a3a of the K/2K/2 modulation. That wavevector is the projection onto the Γ\Gamma-MM axis of the two adjacent K/2K/2 vectors, each of which differs from it by a transverse component of length π/(3​a)\pi/(3a). Detecting or excluding a satellite at |K|/2|K|/2 along Γ\Gamma-KK, as opposed to one at (14,0)(\tfrac{1}{4},0), would establish whether any kagome material realizes the thirty-six-site crystal.

(vi) Parity through nonlinear transport. The C2C_{2} parity that separates the charge order of the metals from the chargon one is, at the MM point, a statement about inversion, and nonlinear transport sorts the two orders by it without a phase-sensitive measurement. A second-order response j∝E2j\propto E^{2} reverses sign under inversion while E2E^{2} does not, so it is forbidden outright for an inversion-even F1F_{1} charge order and symmetry-allowed for an inversion-odd F3F_{3} one. A third-order response is allowed either way. In CsV3Sb5 the third-order longitudinal and Hall responses are large and survive to room temperature, with kinks at the charge-order transition and at the ∼39\sim\!39 K anomaly, while the second-order responses are reported as negligible [20]. That null is what the F1F_{1} assignment of the metals requires, and it fixes the measurement’s sensitivity in the reference material. A doped kagome spin liquid ordering in F3F_{3} should carry a second-order response where the metals carry none, provided the order also breaks threefold rotation and does not cancel between layers. The intrinsic second-order response is governed by the Berry-curvature dipole, a pseudovector in two dimensions, which any threefold rotation annihilates. The signal therefore requires the C3C_{3} breaking of the uni-MM stripe, which the triple-MM and K/2K/2 crystals lack, in domains whose average does not restore C3C_{3}. In a stacked sample an in-plane inversion-odd order can in addition cancel between layers. A second-order null thus excludes the inversion-odd order only where both conditions are established. The null reported for the metals is also in tension with the spontaneous in-plane inversion breaking reported in (i), which was measured in thicker bulk crystals at a higher charge-order temperature, and the two observations have not yet been reconciled.

IX Conclusions and outlook

We have constructed the chargon theory of the kagome Dirac spin liquid and of its ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and chiral descendants, following the analyses of the square [18] and triangular [31] lattices, and the kagome lattice has returned an answer those lattices could not give. The chargon doublet that carries the doped charge is degenerate on the square and triangular lattices, where the interactions decide between superconductivity and density-wave order. On kagome the lattice decides first. The two triangle orientations carry equal flux in the parent ansatz, no symmetry undoes a reversal of that flux, and the doublet splits into a component that disperses in four valleys, the holon band of Ref. [75], and a component whose lowest bands are flat, pinned by the line-graph structure of the lattice (Sec. II.3).
